SPRINGTIME. 0 throstle, sing with all your powers The joy of merry May-time, Awaken bees, and birds, and flowers, , And fill with life the laughing hours, ' It is the children's playtime! For them the bluebells ring their chimes, And wear the bright adorning, And on the chestnuts and the limes A thousand buds unfold betimes, To greet their Mayday morning. Their eager hearts Spring comes to meet v, With light, and song. and blessing; - The daisies nestle at their feet, And violets open fresh and sweet, a"--;:- To feel their warm caressing. To them each primrose haunt is known, Far in the woodland shadows; The joy of Spring is all their own, With all its countless treasure strown Aeross the sunny meadows. We too would join in field and wood
The song that nature raises, And day by day, in childlike mood, Would bless the Giver of all good For buttercups and daisies! ••--3fary Bowies, in Leisure Hour for _Way.

Repentance without amendment is like continually pumping without stopping the leak. "Politeness," says a modern Yankee Socrates, "is awful tender all the world over; it will win nine times out of ten on mankind, and is a good-risk to take even upon the mule." The spirit of liberty is not merely, as some people imagine, a jealousy of our own particular rights, but a I respect for the rights of others, and an unwillingness that any man, whether high or low, should be wronged and , trampled under foot. Delude not yourself with the notion that you may be untrue and uncertain in trifles, and in important things the contrary; trifles make up existence. and give the observer the measure by which -to try us; and the fear- ful power of habit after a time suffers not the best will to ripen into action. Let a man try faithfully, manfully td be right, he will grow daily more and more right. It is at bottom the condition on which all men have to cultivate themselves. Our very walking is an incessant falling, and a catching of ourselves before we come actually to the pavement. It is emblematic of all things a man does. Suspension of judgment at certain times should be . sedulously cultivated. When we remember how fre- quently complex conditions are involved, and how diffi.- - cult it is to understand and appreciate those conditions , and to accord to each its proportionate value, we may well pause and reflect before committing ourselves to judgements which may prove to be-wrong. There is no power of love-so hard to get and keep as a kind voice. A kind hand is deaf and dumb. It may be rough in flesh and blood, yet do the work of a soft heart, and do it with a soft touch. But there is no one thing • that love so much needs es a sweet voice to tell what it means and feels; and it is hard to get and keep it in the right tone. One must start in youth and be on the watch night and day, at-work and play, to get and keep a voice that shall speak at all times the thoughts of a kind heart. An American tourist was inspecting St. Paul's. Lon- don' under the guidance of an Irish verger. Suddenly the latter said, with 'bated breath, "'She surr, 'sh, for we're approaching the tomb of the great Juke—the Juke -of Wiilington, surr. Sure, surr, he loies there; and -undernathe him there's at mate tin tons of granite. And thin comes an iron sarcophagus—and he's in that. And atop o' that, Burr, there's at laste fifteen tons more -of Oirish granite, that's atethe same toime a protection and a mimerial." The American replied, "Well, I guess you've got hint sure. But• if the old fellow shows any signs of breaking out, just-you-cable, at my expense, to Peoria, TELEGRAPHING THE Scemenenne.—When the Prince of Wales was -expected at Niagara -Falls, Mr. Bennett, pro- prietor of the New Fork Herald, instructed his reporter to secure the telegraph wires. This could only be done by keeping them at work on the principle of "First come, first served"; but there was for a time nothing to report. The reporter, therefore, asked what he should do. "Send on the Book of Proverbs," was the reply. The Book of rroverbs concluded, the reporter added to the last verse, No sign of the Prince. What next 9" "Give us Ecclesiastes," was the answer; and the opera- tors were kept at their long and unusual Scripture lesson at a heavy price until the cannon thundered, and the long-expected Heil- of England's Throne came in sight of the great tee-Arse. UNDER FIVE MixrrrEs.—"lf the skin is not kept scrupu- lously clean, effete matters are-retained in the blood; in fact, it becomes poisoned, and health and beauty are simply impossibilities-. the body becomes languid and unfit for much exertion, the brain and mind are far from clear and bright, dreamless -slumber is not obtained, there is hardly an organ of-the body left in good working order, and the complexion 'becomes sallow and the eye muddy. Hence I am -never tired of advocating the use of the bath to my readers. The soap bath is beauty's bath. And it is so simple: a pint of warm water, a bit of the mildest non-scented soap, a lather all over—time, one minuteland a half. A few spongefuls of cold water • applied to:brow and face before entering the shallow bath, then in the bath half a ekeeen spongefuls over the body—time, one Minute only. :Then the towelling— time, two minutes, or under five minutes altogether: This just after getting out Of *bed. How grateful every organ in your body will be! If there be any music in you, you will go singing downetoibreakfast. FENNY-A-LINING EXTRAORDINARY.-011 the grand old principle, "Two can play at that game," a writer in the Saturday Review once undertookto show that he too, if "so disposed," could avoid "calling a spade a spade," with the most grandiloquent of penny-a-liners. Ac- cordingly, he took two Pines from." Comin' through the Rye," and translated them into the•follovving jargon: On the supposition that an individual salutes an individual, Does an individual he wader an obligation to make a stsi-ve- ment of the fact? This, it must be owned, is a tolerable good disguise for the simple query: If a body kiss a body. Need a body tell? But it is nothing to what might be made of it by a man who was bent on doing his best—onworst. See now— "On the hypothesis that an individual member of the human species imprints an osculatory salutation on Hee physiognomy of another individual member of the human species, is it absolutely incumbent on the indi- vidual member of the human species ultimately alluded to, to proclaim that clandestine proceeding in Gath, and publish it abroad in the streets'of AskalonFor the benefit of every individual member of the - widelv-dispersecE family of man in every accessible quarter d the habit-, *bier globe." BREAKFAST: WHAT rr is, AND 'WHAT SHOULD BE.— What a person eats for breakfast often -gives me a due to the state of his health. One example: if while sojourning at an hotel I see a man come 'down to break- fast between ten and eleven, and sit down to devilled kidneys with plenty of sauce (piquant),and perhaps one poor puny egg to follow, I would be willing to aver that he carries a white tongue, and that his liver sadly needs seeing to. Hain and eggs, bacon and eggs, or a beef- steak or underdone chop, with boiled eggs to fellow, and then a cup of nice tea, is a sensible breakfast for a man who is going away out into the fresh air to walk, orfride, or work till noon; but not for a person who has to sit all day in the same position at manual labour. I empha- sise the word manual because intellectual or mental work conduces to appetite. An author hard at his desk, if his ideas be flowing freely, if he be happy at his work, and - time flying swiftly with him, soon gets hungry, which only proves that we must support the body well-when there is a strain upon the mind, so that no extra ex- penditure of tieeue may lead to debility. Cheerful con- •versation insuree the easy digestion of a good breakfast It is a. Pity that-in this country the custom of inviting friendato the matutinal meal is not more prevalent. It may seem a strange thing to say, but I would ten times . sooner go out to tigeakfast than to dinner. One is, or , ought to be, freeheat in the morning; he then needs no . artificial stimulus-to make him feel bright, witty, happy., ,as he too often does.after the duties of the day are over. —"A Family Doctor," Cassell's Family Magacine• `AN AUSTRIAN BAATON ON ENGLISH PRESTIGE IN INDIA.oe can help being moved when he himself sees, in. actual tangible form, -some grand idea of which his only previous conception was denved from reading or hear- say. I saw troops composed of the representatives of -two widely different races, assembled together and mance-wring on the same ground, arrayed underthe same standard, and summoned to serve the same cause, -which is certainly the cause of order and civilisation, but which is also, aed cannot but be above all, that of maintaining the English rule. And certainly to enlist the conquered in the service of the conquerors, when the latter, in point of numbers, form a scarcely perceptible minority. is one of the boldest ideas ever yet conceived in the mind ,of man. Here a world is governed, guided, and kept in ,check by a wand. But behind the material force, which, -if compared with the task it is expected to accomplish, is as nothingeiies the moral force, -which is boundless and incalculable, behind the wand is prestige. So long as it is based on real superiority, prestige has nothing illusory about it. It becomes an illusion when reality ceases to correspond with appearance. There are two enemies to fear—failure, no matter where or whereor against whom, and discussion. Faith does not admit of discussion. -Failure destroys prestige rapidly, though not always completely; diecusskne destroys i secretly, slowly, and effectually. Inasmuch as the sun never sets on the British Empire, the Imperial authorities of tke peninsula of the Ganges are not alone sufficient to maintain English • prestige in India. It can be upheld, impaire& or lost at every point of the glote.—Through the British Empire. .By Baron von Htibzer. Choose always thvvrarthat-seemibest, however rough It may be. Custom will render it easy and agreeable. The class in liatural' History being asked the difference 'between a dog and a tree, the head boy answered :—A tree is covered with bark, while a dog seems to be lined with it." A clever little three-year-old, while her mother was 'trying to get her asleep, became inttrested in some out- side noise. She was told it was caused by a cricket, when she sagely observed, "Mamma, I think he ought to be oiled." In vain he-seeketh others to suppress who bath not learned himself first to subdue. A more glorious victory I cannot be gained over another man than this, that when the injury ben on his part the kindness should begin

on ours. A preacher, whose congregation had begun to fall off somewhat, had it intimated that he would discuss a I family scandal the following Sunday. As a consequence the church was crowded. The minister's subject was "Adam v. Eve." I Whatever weakens your reason, impairs the tender- ness of your conscience, obscures your sense of God, or takes off the relish of spiritual things; in short, what- ever increases the strength and authority of your body over your mind—that thing is sin to you, however inno- cent it may be in itself. I Economy is an abused word. Most people think of it ' as a saving of money, as though to be economical was ! certain, in a sense, to be stingy or mean. Now, economy in its true interpretation is the art of management—is the wise adaptation by which we arrange time, health, and strength so as to produce the best results. 1 The value of anything cannot be measured by its cost or price alone, otherwise the fresh air, cool water, and bright sunshine would be valueless. Two main elements enter into the real value of things ; one is their intrinsic power of producing health, happiness, and life, the other the power of the possessor to use them for that purpose. Only so far as the latter exists and is put forth can the former be made manifest. Soil and seed possess •an inherent power of sustaining life; but, if they are not brought into contact with each other, they are practically valueless. FAMILY UNITY.—The wise parent will not try to make all his children on one pattern in order to perfect his home. He will welcome each separate idiosyncrasy, de- velop each peculiar organisation, and so skilfully culti- vate and blend them together as to infuse the good of each into the whole. His family will thus be a unity, not through similitude, but through mutual love and mutual interest, and the differences which distinguish each will contribute to the more perfect harmony of the whole just as the separate notes of a musical chord combine to form one sweet and harmonious sound. If we are content to do or avoid certain things merely because we are compelled to do so ; if we secretly wish that the constraint were removed, so that we could bound back into opposite courses; if our hearts refuse their allegiance to what our hands seem forced to do— then we may be sure we are not preparing for the law of liberty which awaits all who are able to value it. Good laws and intelligent obedience are the porch and entrance through which we must pass to dwell in the larger and free courts of liberty,, where a beautiful loving loyalty will hold us closer to the right and the good than all penalties, or terrors, or restraints. WHAT A LADY SAYS.—Some of US like to be thin and pale. Interesting and aesthetic we call it; others give it a harsher name; but how to manage it. We are plump, rosy complexioned, biassed with robust health and good appetites, so, consequently, hopelessly girlish, and fresh to look upon. A happy thought strikes us; we drink vinegar and eat lemons—a fact, I assure you. Soon we get thin and flabby, our eyes sunken and lack lustre, ourselves nervous and low-spirited. We get interesting with a vengeance; the dear, good, clever, reliable doctor is called in, and he finds out, after a bit, that our blood is dried up. and when it is too late we leave off lemon eating and vinegar drinking. THE EPISCOPAL RING.—The Episcopal ring is of great antiquity, but its fashion was settled in 1194., when it, was ordained that it should be of solid gold set usually with either a ruby or crystal, in which nothing was to be cut. These were generally used as signet rings, and sometimes for special uses, as when the fonts of baptism were sealed from the beginning of Lent to Holy Satur- day. The newly-made Bishop of the Church of Rome is still invested with a ring by which he is married to the Church. This is always worn on the right hand. A Cardinal's ring is set with a sapphire. The Pope's ring is not worn by him, but is kept for sealing purposes. The ring of the fisherman, as it is called, a signet of steel, is in the care of the Cardinal Chamberlain, and is broken with a golden hammer on the death of a Pope, and a new one made for his successor. THE LONGEST EXISTING WORD.—Far behind most, foreign languages, ancient and modern, comes the Eng- lish language as regards length of words. Except in the word " honorificabilitudinity"—which, though it exists In literature, is, of course, a mere manufactured piece of absurdity—we have, I believe, no word extending beyond seven syllables. To Ame European nations this may appear contemptible enough. In this respect, however, the old world can teach a lesson to the new. In a work to which I hope some time to make a more direct refer- ence, I have met with an Aztec word of thirty-two letters. " amatlacuilelitquitcatla,xlahuilli." It is satis- factory to learn that the signification of the word is worthy of its pr,portions. It means "payment re- ceived for having been bearer of a paper with writing on it." So far as regards the number of letters employed accordingly, we are far more extravagant than the Aztecs. Gallatin, in the "Transactions of the American Ethnological Society," supplies from the Cherokes lan- guage a word even more pretentious. This is " Wini- ta,wtgeginaliskawlungt-anawnelitisesti," which means, '"They will by that time have nearly done granting (favours) from a distance to them and to me." With a vocabulary of this kind a perfect command of speech and writing must be a matter of some difficulty. THE OPERATION TURNED OUT ALL RIGHT.—" I had a xrery funny thing happen to me last week," said one of the leading surgeons of the city in an after-dinner conversa- tion yesterday. "An old coot came to my office, gave ,me the particulars of his case, and wanted a very diffi- • cult, but at the same time short, surgical operation per- formed. He fully understood the situation, and knew that the application of cold steel might be fatal in the end. However, he was ready to take the chances. After the ceremony was over the venerable gentleman gathered himself into his clothes and asked, ' What's the cost of 'this 'ere?' Now, I was playing low-down cunnine.. I knew he was well off and had the reputation of tieing very liberal down'near Antralia. My regular fee would have been fifty dollars, but I had a great head. I re- marked casually that I would leave it to him, when he [unrolled a long wallet and handed me five dols., and a , very old greasy bill it was. There was nobody around to ' kick me, and so I kicked myself. But the next morning the able agriculturist carne•hopping upstairs as lively as ia 4wo-year-old Hambletonian. He slapped down a crisp .100-(101. bill on my table, with the remark,' Hello, Doc! 'what I paid you yesterday was for doin' it. This little hbalance is for knowing how.' "—Chicago Mail.

The bodies of two lovers, Gamuel Jones and Elizabeth Anti Lowe, of Ince, were, on ilonday, recovered from the canal near Henhuret Bridge. MUER AT SEA.—On Saturday, at Winchester Assizes, James vr helan was charged with the murder of George Richardson, second mate of the Nova Scotian brigantine Emma J—Shore, on the high seas on March 15 last. The vessel was on a voyage from New '.:ork to River Plate, and during tbe voyage Richardson found fault with Whelan, threatening to kick him out of the rigging, adding that he would some dark night knock his brains out. It was alleged that the prisoner said he wouid kill the deceased if he came at him again. On the night in question, as the second mate was walking the deck, Wnelan struck him on the head, and pushed him overboard. Pr;souer, on being secured and placed in irons, is alleged to have stated that the mate was "in hell shovelling coals for the devil, and if he could come ,to life again he would kill him as before." The jury found ' him guilty of murder, but recommended him' to mercy • be- cause of the provocation he had received, and the judge passed sentence of death. His Lordship urged Whelan not to build on the recommendation, which, he said he would send to the proper quarter. IMPROVEMENTS IN BUTTER MAKING.—The Waterford butter merchants think it necessary to direct attention to the important subject of making butter. With that view the committee, after careful consideration, ap- proved of the following directions, and they believe that their general adoption will be of the greatest advantage by the improvement that will be effected in the quality of butter, thereby. raising it to the position it ought to occupy, and securing for it a ready sale at remunerative prices in the markets. The milking should be done regularly and carefully, the last drop being taken from each cow, and the hands of the milker should be per- fectly clean. Let the milk be carefully strained, and if the weather be hot the milk should ,be cooled before being "set." This can be done by placing the milk pails in cold water. The milk should be " set "in earthenware or tin vessels and kept in a clean, cool place. Great care to be taken to skim the cream perfectly sweet, and when skimmed not to allow it to get too ripe or sour, as a mis- take of this kind will give a rancid flavour to the but- ter, thereby deteriorating its value fully 50 per cent. Keep the stock -of cream in an earthenware or tinned vessel, and when any fresh cream is added let the cream be stirred, and keep it away from all smells. Let it be carefully covered with muslin to keep it free fromhairs, dust, or dirt. In hot, close weather skimming should be done every twelve or eighteen hours, and in ordinary weather every 48 hours. Churn as often as possible, and the use of the thermometer in the dairy is strongly recom- mended, so that the temperature of the cream and that of the dairy can be ascertained. The proper temperature -for cream before churning is 58deg. to 60deg. Should the cream be too warm, put the vessels in cold water and if too cold, put them in warm water, and while doing so let the cream be stirred steadily to ensure tho- rough cooling or warming as required. When rinsing the cream vessels let it be done with milk, not water. Let the churning be done steadily, and never allow the butter to gather in lumps, as this increases the difficulty of extracting the buttermilk. When churning is com- pleted let half the buttermilk be drawn off, and cold, clean water added, then give-the churn a few slow turns, again draw off half, and add cold 'water ; continue this until the water comes away -quite clear. By following these directions the particles of -butter come away better than if all the buttermilk were drawn off at once. Take the butter from the churn with a skimmer or "sieve," never touching it with the hand. Then place the butter on a table with an incline, to allow of draining. Let the moisture be then pressed out of the butter, .and when it has solidified let it be worked so as to get -rid of all the water and buttermilk. For this purpose we recommend the use of the butter worker, as it does the work easily and regularly, and gives the butter that nice waxy tex- ture so much approved of. When the butters, has been sufficiently worked (care must be taken not to overwork it), let the salt, which should be the finest and the best ob- tainable, be sprinkled over the butter, which should be spread to the depth of half an inch, then rolled up, and worked so as to properly mix the salt. For mild cured butter 11b. of salt to the 561b5., and Whs. to the 701b5., is recommended, and for a "stouter" description of butter double the relative quantities; the eadt to be care- fully measured or weighed. -•- `-"

THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. THE VARIETIES OF THE GAME FOWL. Since cock-fighting has passed away as one of the recognised British sports many of the old game breeds have been lost. These in many cases were merely sports or offshoots from other breeds, and had no great dis- tinctive characteristics to encourage their perpetuation. Breeders of the modern show game fowl confine their attention almost exclusively to four varieties, namely, the black-breasted reds, the brown-breasted reds, the piles, and the duckwings. Occasionally specimens of some other are seen, but they receive no support. Of these four varieties the black-reds, called so for short. are the most popular, and upon this variety has been lavished the skill of some of our most noted breeders. The piles, also, have been very carefully bred, and many of these are simply marvellous in their richness of colour. There can be little doubt that since the abolition of cock-fighting the game fowl has more or less changed in its style and appearance, and probably also in its fight- ing qualities, though it is more than likely rather less in the latter respect than is usually supposed. In some re- spects the change has been a most advantageous one, ;is colour and style have been more bred for. When the difficulties in the way of keeping game fowl are con- sidered it is surprising that they are so popular. These difficulties arise entirely from the disposition of the birds, necessitating that very few shall be kept together, and that all possible precautions be taken to preventthe cocks getting together, or in a very short time injury may be done which can never be remedied. The ordinary breeder can scarcely imagine to what methods the game fowl breeder who has not unlimited space at his com- mand has to resort, in order to accomplish his purpose. Sometimes he has breeding pens and single cocks on a score "walks" as they are called. It is for this reason that the game fowl is not to be recommended to the ordinary breeder. For the production of table fowls it is invaluable as a cross, but except showing were the object in view, we should not advise any one to keep pure game fowls. . The following description of the shape and carriage of the game fowl is from the notes supplied to the "Book of Poultry" by Mr. John Douglass, who may be regarded as the father of the modern show game fowl. In the cock, beak to be strong, slightly curved, and stout where set in the head; head rather inclined to be long, and not round and bullet-shaped; the least possible indent over the eye gives a snake-like appearance which is much admired. Eyes bright red, rather prominent, with a fearless expression. Face, a smooth skin; the throat the same. Ears red, not inclined to white. Neck rather long and a little arched; short hackle, with the points just meeting between the shoulders, but reaching very little on the back. Back flat, wide at shoulders, and narrowing to the tail. Breast round and full. Stern to be clear between the hocks, not let down, but a clear line. Saddle feathers close and short, and not too many of them. Wings strong and not over long, having a great substance at the shoulders; not confined close at the breast, but to be seen detached, as if ready to fly at the first intruder, be he cat, dog, or cock, the points rest- ing over the thighs, but under the saddle. Tail medium length, neither too long or short, but nicely carried; neither squirrel nor drooping, but between the two; not too much spread out, but nicely " venetianed," with about seven secondary feathers each side, the one nicely fitting just above the other; of course the two main sickles about four or five:inches longer than the straight tail. Thighs round, stout, full of muscle, firm, rather long, but well carried in close to the body—not stilty, but so that you can distinguish their form and where set in when facing you. Shanks medium length, nicely rounded, neither flat nor quite round, with a nice clean joint in-setting on to the thigh bone, well standing apart and beautifully scaled. Spurs set low and inclined to point back. Feet flat, toes well spread out, and the hind toe to come straight and flat out from the foot—not, as many do, drooping so as just to put the point to the ground. The latter form is nearly as objectionable as what is termed duck-footed, which is when the hind toe inclißes to point forward the same way as the front toes. The toes should be a good length, and well spread out, with good strong nails. Mr. Douglass's description of the Game hen from the same source is as follows :—Beak to be stout where set on head, curved slightly, and sharp at the point; upper mandible same colour all over—viz., dark horn; comb small, thin, straight and evenly serrated; head rather long, neat, and snake-like; eyes red and prominent, with a fiery expression, as much as to say, "I won't submit ;" face bright red and thin; deaf-ear red and small; wattles thin and neatly rounded; neck inclined to be long, slightly curved, and short-feathered, the feathers meeting at a point between the shoulders when the neck is extended, and not so long as to form a sort of tippet; back in shape similar to the cock, but in the old hen in- clined to be rather more broad and flat, tapering off to the tail; wings not inclined to be long, but to seem short in body, and powerfully made. As these are not birds made for continual flight, they are not so long in com- parison as in a bird of passage, but have very strong butts, and rather short pinion or flight feathers. The wings should be carried rather high, and close in to sides. Tail moderate in length, and nicely " venetianed"—that is, each feather lapping a little over the other, like a venetian blind, to give it a nice neat compact form, not open and fan-shaped. The hen should carry it a little above the horizontal line. Breast broad and prominent; thigh-bone inclined to be long, but well kept close along the body, and not stilty, with great muscle, feeling firm in the hand, so that when you have her in your hand she fills it well up; shank clean and scales smooth: a mode- rate length of bone, finishing off with good, flat,

Tint COLONIAL AND INDIAN FxstintrtoN..—The first week of the Colonial and Indian Exhibition has 13,,en one of complete success. The total numoer of visitors at the close of the peek on Saturday was officially returned at 128 077. The numbers on Wednesday were 12,137, and on Friday 21,078. The first Wednesday at the Isventions Exhibition last year was only 8.243, and the largest previous first Wednesday was in the Fisheries Exhilition-9.198. The first week of the Fisheries had the bemfit of Whitsun Mun- day, and the total ran up to 132,949. The first Friday last year ran up to 12.391. The total for the four days endimt on Friday night was over 94,000, and Saturday was a very full day, for which 25,000 may be taken, in round numbers, so that this year's success will abiut equal the Fisheries without the help of the Whitsun holiday, which will not occur until the middle of June.

spread toes, tho hinder out level toot; carriage upright, • -active., colour of the Black-reds is as follows :—Cock,f and neck-hackles, orange red to the points; back and shoulder coverts, violet red, with a shade of orange; saddle, orange red; breast black, with steel-blue shade all over the breast; tail, rich black, with a slight purple bronze shade in the secondary sickles. In the hen the head and neck are golden, streaked with black. The body colour is partridge, or as near to partridge colour as possible, even to run up the outside or top feathers of the tail; the breast is salmon-red, commencing under the throat, running off a little to ashy colour on the thighs, without the least pencilling on the flight fea- thers in the wings. In the Brown-red Cocks the colour is as follows :—Head and hackle feathers, deep orange red, with a shade of dark in the centre of the feather; shoulder-coverts, dark crimson; saddle, a red maroon on centre, passing to a dark lemon and straw; breast, dark, with a bay streak in the centre of every feather run- ning off on the thighs, which are also streaked with bay; the tail is black ; sickles, narrow and whip-like, and bronzed with a greenish gloss. The breast is gene. rally streaked. In the hen the plumage is dark-brown on the body, with a brassy hackle. In the Duckwing Cock the head is just covered with silver-white small fine feathers; hackle, almost white, only a tinge of straw pervading; his back, a maroon straw and claret; saddle, just a shade darker than the hackle; the shoulders are a nice brassy maroon right from the butts to the steel bar, and no light streaks; the shoulder butts are black, the breast also, and the tail, the latter with a shade of bronze pervading the sickles; the eyes are red, and the legs willow. In the hen the hackle is silver grey, darkly . striped; the breast, a bright salmon red; the back and shoulder coverts, slaty grey. The pile has been well described as being a black red, with the black turned white, and with this alteration the description; of the latter will suffice.

div.head: LTBERAL TEA _PARTY, CONCERT,
div.p: LTBERAL TEA _PARTY, CONCERT,
AND BALL.

Tho annual tea party, concert, and ball in connection with the Liberal party in War - rington were heldon Monday evening in the Public Hall. The hall as usual was suitably deco- rated. Tn front of the organ was the motto " Oros. field for ever" in bold letters, and around the front of the gallery the following mottoes were displayed : " The old ship and the old pilot," "God bless the Grand Old Man," and "Peace and goodwill to Ireland." On the wall opposite the platform was inscribed the wish, " Long life to our President." There were also numerous banners, &c., which gave the hall a bright and pleasing appearance. About 600 persons par- took of tea, the trays being given by the following:— : Mes4rs. Melilinnies, John Crosfield, George Dalin, Thomas Miller, Samuel Barlow, Arthur Browne, John Walker, T. Grime, Mesdames John Rylands, John Burgess, W. Long, Connor, Fleming, Winser, Briggs, John Platt, E. Twiss, James Walker, William Pier. point. P. Caldwell, Greening, J. Haynes, C. S. Burgess, William Robinson, F. A. Roberts. Armitage, Thomas Carter, Broadbent; F. Monks, Gornall, R. Garnett, Yonge, Strange, Jenkins, W. E. Thornton, H. Thorn- ton, 'l'. Morris, and the Misses Harvey and Miss Jones. The following are the names of the tea party com- mittee, viz.:—Messrs. S. Barlow (chairman), W. Roberts (hon. sec.), W. Pierpoint, J. Garner, J. Strange, S. Dunbobbin, W. Bibby, T. Sudlow, J. W. tall, J. Bromley, F. Williams, J. O'Brien, J. Willett, and J. Heywood. After tea a concert was held. On the platform there were Mr. J. Crosfield J.P., Alderman Burgess, J.P., Dr. Gornall, J.P., Mr. W. Pierpoint, Mr. S. Barlow, Mr. J. Winser, Mr. R. Siddall, Mr. R. Stirrup, and Mr. Crosskill. —Mr. H. RORRIITS said they would be sorry to hear that their president, Mr. McMinnies, could not be with them to preside that night owing to ill-health. Mr. Roberts read the following letter from Mr. MoMinnies :—"Summer House, Warrington, May 10.—My dear Mr. Roberts,—l am sorry to say that I am unable to attend the tea party to- night. I am too weak to bear the fatigue, and the objections of my doctor almost amount to a prohibition. I should have been glad to have met the members of the Club and their friends in full numbers, and to have introduced Mr. John Crosfield to the largest meeting of our party since he accepted the position of our candidate. I hope I may be more fortunate in the future, and meanwhile, trusting that you may have a pleasant and successful meeting, I am, yours faithfully, J. G. MoMINNies." (Applause.)— Mr. Roberts then suggested that Mr. John Crosfield take the chair, and this proposal was cordially agreed to. MR. CROSFIRLD, having, amid cheers, taken the chair, said he was very sorry he had to preside in the place of their friend, Mr. McMinnies. He had been with Mr. McMinnies for the last hour, and he certainly was not in a state of health that it would be safe for him to come out of doors. He had, there:ore. urged upon Mr. McMinnies to remain at home, and he told him he would gladly take his place. (Hear, hear.) He (the chairman) was afraid that that tea party had been fixed rather late in the year, and that would account in a great measure for the numbers being smaller than usual at their annual tea party. He was afraid also that the fact of the exhibition opening in Liverpool the next day and her Majesty the Queen coming down to open it had induced a number of their friends to save their money and to go to Liverpool instead of coming to that party. It was very natural that they should do so. (Hear, hear.) He stood before them that night as the selected Liberal candidate for Warrington—(loud applause) —and perhaps they would allow him to say in the first place that it was nets situation of his own seeking, and if he had consulted his own feelings he should have preferred to stop at borne. He was not at all fond of London. It was sadly too big a place for him and he waa;much more at home in Lancashire with Lancashire people. (Hear, hear.) He liked the honesty and independence of Lancashire people. He had been born and brought up amongst them all his life, and when a man got past fifty years of age be was not very fond of change. But still the party said he must stand, and, therefore, he re- plied —" Very well, if you say I must I will." (Applause.) He did not know when the next elec- tion would take place, nobody in England knew, but in his opinion the probability was that there would not be another election this year, because he believed their great leader Mr. Uladstone—(loud applause)—would carry the second read- ing of his Home Rule Bill, and that then in all probability he would withdraw it for the remainder of this session and introduce it in the next session of Parliament. (Hear, hear.) He hoped it would turn out so. They did not, any of them, want another election this year, and it would be much more comfortable in every way to have a fair stand up fight next year. (Hear, hear.) Knowing pretty well the opinions of the members of their own party at all events In this town, he might tell them that he looked forward to the next contest with the greatest confidence. (Applause.) He had not the slightest doubt in his own mind that they should win and win easily. He did not say that because he happened to be the candidate; he said it because of the opinions that they as a Liberal party held that Ireland at last was to have justice done to it. (Loud applause.) As Mr. Gladstone laid it down in his opening speech, a free people ought to be able to make their own laws. That was the principle he should go upon, and if he went to Parlia- ment he could tell them he should support Mr. Gladstone through thick and thin. (Applause.) It was not tassel on that occasion to make political speeches, and he must apol- ogise for having said as much as he had done, but he thought as he was the candidate and that was the first time he had had the opportunity of meeting them they might perhaps like to know a little of the opinions which he held. (Hear, bear.) He should not attempt to address them any further, bat would call upon those who were going to amuse and interest them with their songs, which would be much pleasanter listening to than an old staid speaker like. him- self. (Loud applause). A short but excellent programme was then rendered by well-known vocalists. Miss Booth sang "Kathleen Mavour- neer+ " with excellent effect, and received for it a hearty round of applause. Mr. Littlewood was also well received in the two popular songs "The pilgrim of love" and "The anchor's weighed." which he sang with good taste and clear enunciation. Miss Monks, who becomes more and more a favourite with Warrington audiences, sang "Tit for tat," and, of course, received an encore. In response to the very hearty recall she gave "Home, sweet home,' which was also loudly applauded. The duties of accompanist were ably undertaken by Mr. C. Pigot. Alderman BURGESS in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Crosfield, said he should not allow that opportunity to pass, although politics might be tabooed at a meeting like that, without congratulating MrZCrosfield upon the fact that he bad been adopted by the Liberal party in Warrington as their candidate at the next election. It was a high and dis- tinguished honour, and no doubt Mr. Crosfield felt it So; and tbat wheu the time came when he would be required to enter upon the contest they would find him a most ener- getic and able candidate. (Applause.) Alderman Burgess also included in the vote of thanks those who had taken part in the concert, those who had so generously given trays, and the ladies who had prepared and eerved'Ohe edibles, aim Mr. S. Ben Low said that it was with great pleasure that he seconded the vote of thanks proposed.byfAlderman Bur- gess. He was sorry that Mr. McMinnies was not able to be present to add to the enjoyment of the occasion. The ladies who had provided for the entertainment had done their duty remarkably well, andi were deserving of the heartiest thanks. Every time they had heard their candidate he seemed to speak better, and he (Mr. Barlow) hoped that in a very short time they would hear him speak in the House of Commons. (Applause.) The proposition was then carried with applause. The CHAIRMAN, in reply, briefly returned thanks on his own behalf, and also on behalf of those included in the vote of thanks. He was very much obliged to them for the compliment, and must be allowed to refer to what Mr. Bar- low said about his (Mr. Crosfield's) being the future mem- ber for Warrington. He remembered that at the last elec- tion, whilst the votes were being counted, Mr. Barlow came to him at about seven o'clock in the evening, and said "We have won ;" but he was mistaken then, and he might be mistaken again. In entering into the contest they must do their duty to the best of their ability, and then he had not the slighest hesitation in saying what the result would be. (Cheers.) On the conclusion of the concert the room was cleared for dancing, which was indulged in until the early hours of 1 the following morning. There was a large number present. The band fer dancing was provided by Air. Thomas Knight,

of Latohford,and gave unqualified Patisfaotion ; and suitable I :efreshments were supplied by Ma. E. J. Mitchell, the , rnamger of the Liberal Club. Mr. W. Bibby ably under- took the onerous duties of M.C. The whole of the arrange- ments were under the personal superintendence of Mr. Barlow, the chairman of the committee, and Mr. William Roberts, hon. sec., and these gentlemen are to be congratu- lated upon their success. The dancing was kept up with spirit and all present appeared to thoroughly enjoy themselves.

NEW BOOKS, &c.

Gustave Flaubert's "SalammbB" Englished—that is the new word—by M. French Sheldon, has already made pome stir, as published by Messrs. Saxon and Co., London, and is destined to make more for it has al- ready reached a second edition. It is truly an ex- traordinary work, aad is not unnaturally regarded by the admirers of the great French author as his masterpiece. It is a novel—a wonderful novel and a not less wonderful history. It deals with a period in the history of Carthage which historians have somewhat neglected; and while presenting the war- like events of that period with btarkling vividness, the power of love is made manifest in a way that enthrals the reader. The introductory memoir, by Mr. Edward King, gives an interesting account of the brief but brilliant career of Flaubert, and refers to the historical groundwork of the story. Salammbo, the heroine of the novel, is the daughter of Hamilcar Berea, and the half-sister of Hannibal, who, how- ever, figures as a mere boy. The "grand passion" for Salammb6 becomes the motive of astion in Mdtho, and its o'er-ma-tering effect upon the bar • barian who struggles against Barca is delineated , with marvellous skill. Flaubert reveals in every page an extraordinary knowledge of the men and manners of the period, and we can imagine archeo- logists enjoying the feast which is spread before them without the least regard to the story as a story. Mr. H. M. Stanley, to whom the translation is dedicated, says:—" I do not know of any volume of its size that conveys so many particulars of the manners, customs, usages, household effects, methods of worship, military tactics, and sieges of any nation as this furnishes us of the Carthaginians." There is ,much indeed that is" cruel and inhuman" to record ; but Flaubert recognised that if we would profit by the teachings of history we must above all things get, if possible, at th 3 truth. The style of the work is thoroughly characteristic; it is alive at every point. It is the reverse of diffuse; it is graphic and vivid, and yet compressed. The reader's imagination is stimulated and then taken captive. M. Sheldon has had a difficult task as translator, but he has on the whole done his work well, for his labour has been a labour of love.

"The Irish Parliament; What it was an. 4. What it did," is a valuable little work from the pen of Mr. J. G. Swift Mac Neil, M.A., just issued by Messrs. Cassell and Co. It treats in successive chapters of the constitution of the Irish House of Lords and House of Commons; the relation to the Crown of England ; and to the English Parliament; and there are separate chapters on the relations of the Irish Parliament to the English and Irish Privy Councils before and after 1782. Another section deals with Irish administration, and a clear account is given of the points of difference between the laws and practice of the English and the Irish constitutioas. It need hardly be said that a treatise of this kind, written as this is by a competent authority in a dis- passionate style, is of especial use at the present moment when the question of a new Parliament for Ireland is before the country. Mr. Gladstone, in commending the work on the Irish Parliament. directed attention to" the way in which material iejuries were inflicted upon Ireland through commercial or anti-commercial arrange- ments ;" and the result is another treatise by Mr. Mac Neill with the title of "English Interference with Irish Industries." It furnishes a painful chapter of Irish history ; but it is one which must be studied by those who would put themselves in a position to understand the Irish people. Mr. Chaplin is not an authority who would be likely to err on the side of exaggerating the sufferings of Ireland; but, refer- ing some time ago to the fact that Irishmen were now-a-days mainly dependent upon the land for their support, he said: "It was not always so; there were other industries in Ireland in former days which flourished, and flourished to a considerable extent until they first aroused, and were afterwards sup- pressed by, the selfish fears and commercial jealousy of England." The late Mr. Fawcett, speaking in 188 r on the same topic, said: "A mass of vexati- ous restrictions were imposed on her industry • and it was thought that if any branch of Irish trade in- terfered with English profits that branch of Irish trade was immediately to be discouraged." It is the object of the work before us to explain in detail how all this was done, and how it has operated not only to cripple the resources of Ireland but to heighten the feeling of hostility to England which had previously been engendered by generations of oppression. The author is careful to give authorities for his state- men.t,s ; and, as official documents and speeches are largely quoted in both works it will be seen that they are valuable as books of reference on the burning question of the Government of Ireland. " Cassell's book of Sports and Pastime" is being issued in parts of 6d each, and will be completed in 15 parts. It describes as many as 6co different games, and offers so much in the way of amusement for all weathers as to make one wish one could always be a boy. Part I to hand treats of cricket, football, tennis, golf, and riding, and it is amply illustrated. "The World of Wonders" is also being issued in parts (6d each) by the same firm. A glance at the contents of this fascinating book is sufficient to sug- gest that the world has been ransacked in order to pro-. dnceit ; fur science and art—every element and every clime—are laid under contribution. The illustrations, are a cardinal feature in a work of this kind, and as to this it is sufficient to say that they sustain Messrs. Cassell's high reputation. "Familiar Wild Flowers (part 3) is adorned with coloured plates of the apple blossom and the borage flower. The pictures are charminely finished, and the text gives all that the general reader can desire to know. Part 21 completes the fine-art edition of Long- fellow, which has been so much admired. The first volume is to hand of Hood's poems in the miniature library. It is like the rest in this series—neatly bound, beautifully printed, and in every way dainty. "Thoughts on the present Discontents" and speeches by Edmund Burke constitute the latest volume to hand of Cassells National Library—that wonderful iiiBllfl of books at threepence each. "The Magazine of Art" for May has for its fron- tispiece a fine engraving of John Constable's celebra- ted painting "The Hay-wain." There is an article ongauildford, which is described and illustrated in a way which is likely to cause Courists to pay it a visit, even when it is a little out of their way. "The Ro- mance of Art." gives in detail the story of the " Cot- tage Countess" so dear to song and tradition. Amongst other more noteworthy papers there is one on "Celtic Metal-work' and another on "Some Eng- lish Carriages," both of which are suitably illus- trated.

The current issue of Cassell's Magazine contains amongst other attractive things an article on Mr. Proude's "Oceans," with a good portrait of Mr. Fronde. The Family Doctor discourses on "What it really means," and Mr. A. Holt tells us something of "The pastime of archery." The two serial stories are in full swing and lose nothing of interest. "The Quiver "opens well with an illustration of " a group gone a-naming " and picture of the Martyr's child, both of which are capitally executed. The "Short Arrows" are also well pointed with illustration. Amongst the longer " arrows " may be mentioned "The Resurrection Miracle" by Rev. Dr. Bona; " Navvydom in the North" by Mrs. Garnett, and "The science of Silence" by the Rev. E. J. Hardy. "Little Folks" ia, as ever, merry and wise, and prettily illustrated. " Gleanings from Popular Authors" (part 9) main- tains its high standard alike as to text and illustra- tion. Part Four of Cassell's "Illustrated Shake- speare" is devoted to" The Merry Wives of Windsor." Old Falstiff is admirably hit off. The EnyclopaAio Dictionary (part 28) wanes the reader through the letter D and on to E. "The Book of Health,' (part 25) treats of the eye and sight and of the ear and hearing. "The English Illustrated Magazine" leads off with a fine engraving of a delightful May landscape by Mr. J. MacWhirter, A.R.A. "In Umbria ' "Sir Roger de Coverley," and "Bird Life in South gweden" are well illustrated ; and there is a very readable paper on Nell Gwynn." We have also to hand the current issues of Ward and Lock's "Technical Journal and Industrial Self-instructor ;" and the following journals of dress and fashion:—" The Season," "Le Moniteur de la Mode," " Myra's Journal," "Myra's Threepenny Journal," and Mrs. Leach's "Family Dressmaker."

THE GREEK CRISIS. BLOCKADE OF PORTS.—MOVEMENT OF TROOPS. RESIGNATION OF THE MINIS [Jilt. VIENNA, SUNDAY.—TOe declaration of the Powers, noti- fying the beginning of the blockade of all the H,llenic ports, Vas handed to M. Delvannis yesterday. The document was signed by England, Germany, Austria, Russia, and Italy. Anetrers, SllNDAY.—lmmediatelv after receiving notifica- tion of the blockade from the Charges (2,' Affaires of the Great Powers, the Greek Government telegraphed to all the Cheek ports to stop the issue of the usual ships' papers, and requested the authorities to notify that all Greek vessels leaving port would do so at their own risk. Three ste imers leaving the Pirteus to-day were obliged to turn beck owing to the blockade. The action of the Powers created a stir in financial and commercial circles, but the general public ap- Nand indifferent. The General commanding on the fron- tier reports that a Ge-eek outpost fired several shots yester- day evening upon the Turkish outposts at Platomona, near the same place where a similar incident occurred recently. The Turks fell back. rile General adds that the Greek soldiers were arrested and punished; and tranquillity is now restored. Later in the day it was annonnced that the Ministry had tendered their resignations to the King. who refused to accept them. His Majesty has written a letter to M. Delyannie, declaring that the Premier will be held responsible for the present condition of Greece. Another battalion left to-day for the front. LONDON, SUNDAY —The Duke of E linbargh has now es- tablished a strict blockade of the Greek Dorts alone the east toast, in accordance wi-h the terms of the notification de- livered to the Hellenic Government by the Charges d'Affaires of the allied Powers. His R. er,E;l Highness has Over forty, vessels of the international fleet protecting the zone, into and from which ne Greek ships, whether men- of-war or merchant vessels, will be allowed to pass.—Press Association. ATHENS, MONDAY.—M. Delvannis, at hi 3 audience with the King to-day, persisted in his resignation, and declared that if it were not accepted he would band over to his Majesty the seals of office and withdraw. The King there- fore summoned M. Tricoupis, who represents the minority in the Chamber, but the leader of the Oppo- a.itien declined the task of forming a new Cabinet, stet- leg that the country being constitutional the choice of Government should come from the Chamber and not from the King. •CARIDIA, TOESDAY.—The international let, which left tt,cla Bay for PiraPna on the 9,h mat, bet Was compelled through stress of weather to return to the Bay, sailed again 'this morning. CONsTaNTINOPLE, TIIESDA.Y.—Although diseemement is expected immediate'y, intelligence has nevertheless been received here that b )(lies of Greek irregulars are being 'formed and' are advancing towards the Turkish frontier. The Porte has brought these movements under the notice of the Powers. The Porte is concluding an arrane.:e- ment with the Ottoman Beak for an advance of £750,000 Turkish. ATHENS, TIIESDAY..M. Delvannis proves obdurate. He .distinctly declines to remain in. the Minie'ry or to convoke] the Chamber. The King has accepted the resignation of the Government, and all probabilities point to M. Rikakie undertaking the task of forming a new Minibtry. Lest night M. Delyannis had a conference with the deputies belongiug to his OEM party, to whom he explained why he persisted in resigning. lie declared that only war could enable Greece to hold up her head again as a nation, and to wipe Out recent humiliations. Bnt such a serious step was im- possible without the full and unanimous consent of the Country. Unfortunately the agitation of the Opposition and the indifference of Royalty had paralysed the efforts Q( the patriotic party. Tiv, speech was well received. FORMATION OF A NEW CABINET. ATHENS, WEDNESDAY, 12-30 PM.M. Papetnichalo- 'potties had an interview with the King this morning, at which he submitted to his Majesty the names of the pro- Posed new Ministers. The King, however, desired that the Cabinet should be a provisional on for summoning the Chamber. M. Papemichaloolulos, diesenting from this view, finally declined to accept office. The King has now sum- moned M. Valvis to form a provisiensl Cabinet and con- voke the Chamber, which should pronouace upon thechoice of the new Ministry. The Chamber, however, cannot meet earlier than ten days hence at least, and such a prolonga• ton ef the crisis would Cause great prejudice to the country, as the blockade will cleubtl-se be maintained until a stable Government is formed to defer to the wishes of Europe. Hopes are still entertained that a new Ministry may be formed to-day. Count de Molly's departure for Paris has been postponed until to-tnorrow. ATHENS, WEDNESDAY, 4-40 VAIiS has seeceeded in forming a Cabinet. He takes the office of Minister of Justice as well as that of Premier, and the other pertfolios are distributed as follows : —General Pettnezes, Minister of War ; M. Miadiiis, Minister of Marine ; M. Louriotis, Minister for Foreign Affairs ; M. Avierinoo, Minister of Finance ; M. Verizelos, Minister of Education ; M. Pa- pailiopulos, Minister of the Interior. The Ministers have gone to the Palace to take the oath of office. • The Greek Minister paid a long visit to Lord Rosebery at the Foreign Office on Wednesday, and afterwards Count Ilatzfeldt, the German Ambassador called. div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 15, 1886

appeal to Lord Hartingten to disclose his pleas. Had not the time come when they should know his poliey ? Was it to be the plan which was proposed to the Loyalist.' of Belfast in November, when the noble lord said he should not otajeet to "a greed and bold reconstruction of the Irish Government?" The Government might be daring, but they were not so daring as the man who undertook to re- construct the Irish Government without touching the legis- lative difficulty. A man who proposed to do that was either a magician or a man who was not much accustomed to the practical transaction of political affairs. He was sorry to think that since November last his noble friend had not gone forward but rather backward. He owned he did not believe in his noble friend's method of dealing with the Irish dill- culty. They ought not to cast the fate of Ireland into the lottery of politics, but to eolve the problem once for all. (Cheers.) The Marquis of lIARTINOTON, who was loudly cheered, moved the rejection of the bill. He said he believed it to be a mischievous measure, and one which would not heal the long-standing feud between Groat Britain and Ireland. It dire not satisfy any of the essential conditions laid down ty the Premier himself, and it was not a final settlement. There was. nothing in it which specially commended itself to Liberal principles; and, holding these opinions, he and his friends had thought it right net to conceal them, but openly to state them and take means to give effect to them. He did not think he was called upon to give an alternative policy, but he believed there were many reforms which could be made in the highly centralised but yet somewhat non-efficient system of government in force in Ireland. The Houseat large was entitled to know before voting on the bill whether it was to be regarded merely as an abstract resolution or a bill which was intended to pass into law. His lordship did not know whether the announcement just ' made would remove the hostility of Mr. Chamberlain, whose objections did not stop at the question of Irish representation at Westminster. There were in the bill principles of far greater importance than were contained in any dozen or- dinary bill. An authority was to be created, for the first time, which could limit the authority of Parliament. The cardinal principle laid down by Mr. Gladstone of the unity of the Empire was not secured. We might for a time after the passing of the bill maintain a semblance of unity when opposed to foreign nations, but internally our unity would have disappeared. The safeguards for the minorities in Ireland were worth nothing, and it was probable that in a few years there would be a successful agitation for the removal of the last of the provisions intended for the protection of the minority. In conclusion, Lord Hartington quoted the language of Mr. Gladstone in 1881, when be condemned the Irish party as the preacl,ers of a " doctrine of public plunder," and spoke of the resources of civilisation not being exhausted. The principles advecated now by that party had not much changed, and it was no argument for a radical change of policy that that party had been largely augmented in the House. He recommended now the policy then favoured by Mr. Gladstone, and strongly disapproved of the policy of retir- ing weakly from "the conflict between law on the one hand and sheer lawlessness on the other." (Cheers.) Mr. O'BRIEN (editor of "United Ireland ") said the Irish people and the Irish race throughout the world regarded the bill as a treaty of peace, which they would loyally ob- serve and keep. He pointed to the changed condition of Irish feeling towards Lord Spencer and Mr. Gladstone since the era of conciliation set in as showing the advisableness of advancing in the same path.—The debate was con- tinued by Mr. S. Hoare, Mr. Fletcher, Mr. A. Bartlett, Mr. Jordan, Lord Ebrington, and Mr. C. Lewis.—Sir H. JAMES moved the adjournment of the debate, which was agreed to. The House adjourned at a quarter past two o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. SCOTCH SALMON FISHERIES.—The Marquis of HUNTLY moved the second reading of the Salmon Fisheries Amend- ment (Scotland) Bill.—Lord BALFOUR condemned the bill as being enterely one-sided, and its provisions in flagrant dis- regard of the interests of all except those who were purely upper proprietors. ENGLAND AND BURMAIL MANDALAY, SIINDA.Y.—Seme excitement has been caused by the arrest in Rangoon on a charge of complicity in the insurrectionary movement at Henz4dali of Kooungbah. the wealthiest Burmese merchant in Mandalay. He was for many years the confidential broker to the Bombay and Bar- mah Company. THE AMERICAN STRIKES. - CHICAGO, SIINDAS.—The authorities here declare that they have evidence to prove that the prisoner Fisckea, if IVA the principal instigator of the Socialist outrage upon the police on the 4th inst ,is at least an accessory to the affair. The police continee their search for anarchists. CANADIAN FISHERIES QUEATION.—THE SEIZURE OF AN AMERICAN STEAMER. OrrAwA, MONDAY.—Tbe roaster of the American fishing echooner David Adams. which was recently seized by the Canadian authorities for buying bait in the harbour of Digby, Nova Scotia. will be proceeded against in Nova Scotia Courts for the violation of the Canadian Customs and Fisheries Acts, and for the infraction of the convention of 1818. WASHINGTON, MONDAY.—Numefons resolutions were ic- troduced in the House of Representatives to-day recom- mending an inquiry into the circumstances of the seizure of the American schooner, David Adams. Resolutions in favour of an inquiry into the seizure were also proposed in the Senate. EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. WADY HILFA, WEDNESDAY.—The Egyptian general, Juf,seh Peeha rriehudo, has arrived here, and is actively engaged in receiving deputations from the Arab tribes with the obkict of arranging terms of peace. AMERICA. ARREST OF HERR MOST. NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY.—Iierr Most, the Anarchist leader, and formerly editor of the Freiheit, has been ar- rested. According to latest advices from Kansas City, twenty- four perscns were killed during the storm there yesterday. TERRIBLE S rORMS IN SPAIN AND

AMERICA. MADRID, TIIURSDAY.—A gale of extraordinary violence, accompanied by hail, occurred here yesterday evening causing serious havoc, especially in the outskirts of the city., A portion of a church tower was blown down. Several people were killed, and many others injured. Telegraphic comtnnnication was also interrupted. MADRID, TIIIIRSDAY, 11.30 A M.—About 70 persons were killed and 200 injured by the hurricane last night. Several c,untry houses have also been destroyed in villages near Madrid. Owing to the interruption of telegraphic com- munication no news has been received from the provinces, but the hurricane is expected to have caused widespread devastat ion. NEW You, THURSDAY.—CycIones continue to prevail in the Western States. Telegraph wires have been blown down everywhere, and telegraphic communication with Cincinnati is entirely cut off. Terrific storms of wind and rain are reported from Pittsburg and Cleveland and the sur- rounding districts. A Central News telegram, dated New York, 'Thursday, says terrible cyclone is reported to have burst yes- terday over Ohio, the towns of Dayton and Xenia being devastated. Many lives are reported to have been lost, but it was impossible to gather definite details yet, all the surrounding telegraph wires having been wrecked in the storm. The starm which wrecked the northern part of Kansas City, Missouri, caused the death of 24 persons, including 15 pupils of the Lithrop school, while many others were injured.

B. HARNESS. seven o'clock. THE MEDICAL BATTERY COMPANY, LIMITED, HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Txurtseeev. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. 52, OxFORD-STREET, LONDON, W. THE HOME RULE DEBATE. Sir H. JAMES resumed the debate upon the motion for the second reading of the Irish Government Bill, remarking at the outset that the judgment he had exercised on the sub- ject had been unaffected by any influence cr motive except a desire to arrive at a just conclusion. He understood that the Prime Ministeir took the view that any measure he in- troduced on the subject must be subject to five conditions, and he (Sir Henry) contended that if this measure became law it would not fulfil one of those conditions. One condi- tion was the unity of the empire, and another the supremacy of Parliament. The unity of the law was essen- tial to the unity 'of the Empire. They were asked to say that there should be no united Parlia- ment dealing with England and Ireland, and the moment they removed the United Parliament they would remove all that constituted union between the two coun- tries. If the bill passed Ireland would be brought lower than any colony of this countre, for it would have no army, no navy, no commerce, and he did not believe the Irish would accept that as a final settlement. He believed tbeir object was to obtain final separation, and they would be giving them the opportunity of securing that separation if they passed this bill. He insisted that the demand for an alternative plan threw an unfair responsibility upon anyone who might differ from the Government. Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNER/lAN, dealing with the arguments of Sir H. James as to the unity of the Empire, said the Go- vernment had • consulted the highest authorities, and had been assured that under the bill the supremacy of Parlia- ment was maintained. When the Liberals took office there were two courses open; they might have endeavoured to suppress the National League, or they might have yielded to the just aspirations of the Irish people. To suppress the League was easier said than done. If they undertook to suppress that they must attack political opinion. Such a policy was not only unwise, but impracticable. Then they must give ta the Irish people in one form or other the self- government they desired. On the question of the retention or non-retention of the Irish members at St. Stephen's they were ready to consider with the most friendly mind all the suggestions that might be made. They were anxious to find some way of recenciliag the main points of the bill with the views expressed by their friends. He was a firm believer in the sobering effect of direct responsibility, and he was equally a firm believer in the healing effects of joint and equal co-operation in public life among men of all creeds and classes in the State. Mr. E. CLARKE considered that tbe new proposal of Mr, Campbell-Bannerman did but make "confusion worse con- founded."—Mr. J. REDMOND asserted that in the judgment of the Irish representatives the bill provided a final settle- ment of the question.—Mr. BOYD KINNEAR held that Ulster men had as much right to say they would not come under the proposed Constitution as the Nationalist members bad to say that they would. His plan for the settlement of the Irish question was to give to Ireland equal justice with England and Scotland —The debate was corrinued by Lord G. tiatnilton, Mr. Dillon, Mr. Leathern and Mr. Bernard Coleridge. On the motion of Sir R. Cross the debate was adjourned till Monday next. The House adjourned at 1-15 a.m.

THE ROCK FERRY MURDER CASE.—At Chester Assizes, on Thursday morning, Robert Travis, hotel keener, of Sut- ton, near Chester, was again placed on his trial charged with the wilful murder of Jane M'lntyre, wife of a sea captain, living at Rock Ferry, on February 13th. The court was again deirsely crowded. His Lordship said that Mrs. .ii.`lntyre appeared to be on friendly terms with all about her, and there could be no doubt that she came to her death by violence. Now, who was there in the room who could have done this. There were only two persons—the prisoner at the bar and Platt. It was impossible that there were , two men in the house, as Travis bad said in one of his statements, for no one was found in the house and no one could have escaped, because the doors bank and front were securely fastened from the inside. It was impossible, there- fore, to resist the conclusion that the deed was done by some one in the house, and the only two persons there, as he had already said, were the prisoner and Platt. The jury retired at ten minutes to one o'clock and returned into court at twenty minutes to two o'clock. In reply to the clerk of arraigns the jury announced a verdict of guilty, accom- panied by a recommendation to mercy. Mr. Justice Haw- kins then pronounced fmntence of death, and the prisoner was assisted from the dock. COAGULINE.—Cement for Broken Articles, 6d. Is, 2e: /aostage 2nd. Sold everywhere. RUGBY RULES. WARRINGTON T. MANCHESTER ( was generally thought that the Wakefield Trinity match was the last orthe season, but to the astonishment of many about Wednesday last this was found to be incorrect, as a match had keen arranged between the above teams for the benefit of the Warrington first team. In the morning rain steadily fell, but at the time of starting the weather bad taken a turn for the better. A counter attraction in the shape of a cricket match was also one of the features of the day ; but was in no way accountable for the moderate number of spectators who had assembled to witness the preceedines, and who at the time of starting numbered about 1,000. Dating the week it was rumoured that a very powerful team was coming to oppose the Warrington lads, including players from Swinton. Broughton, Broughton Rangers, &c., but when the team arrived this was found not to be the case, although a rather strong team had been scraped together, including some such well known players as Maclean (Broughton), Hayward (Broughton). Haselden (Manchester Rangers), Mason (Ambleside), Bainbridge (Free Wanderers), but who could not withstand the good combination and. passina as shown by Warren's lads. The Warrington .for- welds had evidently taken a lesson from the previous week's performance by the celebrated Wakefield Trinity team, as a most decided improvement was witnessed in their ranks. The ground, which had been very hard during the week, was at the time of starting in splendid condition owing to the morning's rain. Spinning for the choice of goals, Harry Ashton with his usual luck lost the toss. Frank Turner kicking off against a slight wind, the bat going into touch. By strong forward play the oval was tsken to the visitors' 25, and in a few minutes a dead ball resulted, after some strong kicking by the home forwards. Hayward first showed up prominently on behalf of the Man- chester team. He went through a scrimmage in fine style and relieved to half-way, Maclean further seconding his efforts by a dash through the scrimmage, and shortly after- wards the same player saved a good rush on the part of the Warrington forwards, and nicely kicked to touch. The home forwards rushed the ball to the visitors' 25, but their forwards being on the alert again took play to half-way. Jolley next made a dashing run, being only collared when in the visitors' 25. Harry Ashton taking possession, passed very nicely to W. Dillon, who ran in, and planted the hall right behind the posts. Barnes was entrusted with the place, and kicked a magnificent goal. From the kick- out a rattling good scrimmage took place, Mason obtain- ing a free kick from a punt by Jolley. Play for some time was confined to half-way, scrimmages being the order of the day. Haselden relieved the monotony of the proceed- i.ngs.by a good rua to the home 25, the home forwards tak- ing it back again. Maclean, however, was not to be denied, for, with a fine rush, he took the oval to the home 25. Barnes than obtained a piss which was intended for Hasel- den, and gained a lot of ground, being well seconded by Ashton and W. Dillon. Buxton tried a d-op at goal, the forwards thinking that a premier point had been gained. Front the drop out Hewitt handled the ball for the first time, and nicely returned it to touch. The same player shortly afterwards relieved ftom a scrimmage, and Fair. Turner made a dashing run, nothing much, however, being gained, owing to some loose passing. Good kicking was then indulged in by Gilbert, Buxton, and Skinner, and in the end a free kick was accepted by Gilbert. Jolley subse- quently tackled Haselden in grand style, and Buxton ob- taining Possession ielieved 0 25. -The good forward play of the visitors took the oval to half-way, and same excellent passing was witnessed, Buxton, Barnes, and Jolley being the recipients, and the play was confined to the line. Hasel- den, however, relieved to half-way, and the visitors' forwards seconded his efforts, the play raging in the home 35. Chiefly through the aid of Barnes and Ashton play was taken to half-way, and Haselden obtained a free kick, which was charged down by Ashton, end further supplemented by a dribble by Frank Turner. Half-time was then called with the ball in the home 25, and on re- suming it was kicked into touch; but Speakman, by a grand effort, removed the play to the centre, and on being collared passed the ball to Barnes, who took it to the 25. Estcourt, however, removed it to half-way, and IL Boardman replied with a run and kick equally as good, and play settled down in the visitors' 25. A fine pass by Gilbert was the next item of interest. and Barnes dropped a magnificent goal amidst load cheers. The kick-off was charged down by W. Dillon, Allen being next to the fore by a good dodgy run. An excellent kick by Jolley and a follow up by Fair Turner removed play to half-way, and some good kicks were then indulged in by Skinner and Boardman, nothing much, how- ever, being gained. By strong forward play and chiefly through the efforts of Maclean and Haselden, the contest was taken to the line, the Manchester contingent scoring tl eir first and only minor point. From a kick out Higgin- bottom obtained a free kick, and play for a short time raged in the home quarters, Fair.l urner relieved by astrong rush, immediately afterwards being well tackled by Skinner. Barnes afterwards obtained possession and succeeded in getting over the line. Speakman failed to land a grol from a very difficult place, and Gilbert returned the kick-out, whilst

Jolley made a niee ran, play being again confined to the visitors' line. Skinner went to the relief with a strong run and kick, and good forward play on the part of the visitors compelled the teams to struggle near the centre. A clean piece of passing was afterwards witnessed on the part of Boardman, Ashton, Dillon. and Davies. Mason, however, frustrated their efforts to score by saving in grand tvle..and shortly afterwards the same player ran back to touch down. Barnes hag now a chance to score but preferred to take his drop at goal, a minor being the result. By good forward play on the part of the visitors the struggle raged in the home 25, but Buxton put in a splendid run, and play was confined to the visitors' 25, where it remained ure til the referee blew his whistle, thus bringing to an end a very pleasant and enjoyable game, the last of the season. ; On the part of Warrington Barnes was in rare form, and on Saturday passed rather better than for some weeks. Buxton played his little in a masterly way and once was within an ace of dropping a goal. Jolley just now is in clinking form, and the way in which he played this (the last match) puts his mistakes during the past stason in the shade. If Board- man and Hewitt had little to do, the two half backs showed a vast improvement on the previous week's performance, but it must be remembered that they then had for their opponents two of the best half backs in the kingdom. Of r the forwards W. Dillon'a play was really splendid. Very little has been said of this player's performances during the ' past season, but for good honest hard work there is not a better man in the team. He was well seconded by Davies, Ashton, and Heyes. In the visitors' ranks Haselham was out and out the best back, his best seconders being Mason and Allen. Coming to their scrimmagers, Maclean centinuallY led his partners, tackling in a praiseworthy manner and saving well; Hayward, Bambridge, and Hiegingbottom were able supporters. Teams (17 each) :—Warrington : Back. Hewitt ; thrPe•quarter backs, Jolley, Buxton, Barnes, and Boardman; halfbacks, Gilbert and Speakman; forwards, Hayes, Davies, Fair. Turner, F. Tnrner, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, Hough, Littlevrood. Povev, and Ashton (captain). Man- chester District : Back. Skimmer (Birch); three-quarter backs, Allen (Sale), Faeelham (Manchester Rangers), and Estcourt (Sale); half backs, Mason (Ambleside), and Wilkintrm (Sale) ; forwards. Bainbridae (Free Wanderers), Beck (Birch), H. A. H.ggingbottom (Birch), W. Rigging. bottom (Birch), Walker (Birch), Mclean and Hayward (Broughton), Galey, Pollard, and Haselham (Manchester Rangers), and Marks (Ardwick). Mr. E. Warren discharged his duties as referee in a satisfactory manner. Mr. T. Barnes and Mr. J. Bramhall were the umpires.

WELLINGTON CHALLENGE CUP COMPETITION: SEMI- FINAL TlE.—The semi-final tie of the Wellington Football Challenge Cup was played on the ground of the Earlestown club, the Mesnes, on Saturday afternoon. The contesting teams were the Stubsbaw Cross Wanderers (Ist) and the Earlestown club 2nd team. There was a considerable num- ber of spectators who were rewarded by witnessing a splen- didly contested game. During the first half the Earlestown 2nd played down hill, but though they had the best of the play, they failed to score, while their opponents notched a single point. On the change of ends the home team played splendidly, and raised the enthusiasm of their supporters by storing a victory of four goals to one.—The final tie of the competition will be played by the first and second teams of the Earlestown club, and as the " juniors " have been show- ing good form of late, many of their supporters expect them to secure the trophy—at present held by the first team.
