The Lancashire County eleven met 22 Colts at Werneth on Friday in last week. The great aim of the Lancashire I executive is to find a good swift bowler and in this instance they were unsuccesssul. The Celts last week end were only a moderate let, the best being J. N. Woodhouse (Staley). A. Smlth Oldham), and M. Lawton (Bloorside), Smith being far away the best man. Eight of the Australian men were again tusy in club matches on Saturday, five—Scott, Bruce, Mcllwraith, Trumble, and Garratt—for Broadwater against Esher, and three—Evans, Blackham, and Palmer—for Lausanne against Spencer. For the Broadwater Club, all the Colonists got I into double figures, except Mcllwraith. who, however, made I up by effecting- three splendid catches in the long-field. The Broadwater innings closed for 261. Esher made a sorry show against the bowling of Garratt, who secured seven wickets at a cost of 59 runs. The other two Colo- nials tried, Bruce and Trumble, were not successful. The Esher innings only made 140 runs. In the other match the distinguished visitors were not tl the fore with the bat, Blackham being the only one to get into double figures (28). With the balj, however, they were quite the opposite. A few runs were hit off Evans, but Palmer completely puzzled the batsmen, and when the eleventh man returned to the pavilion only 29 runs had been made. Palmer's average at the close read-9 °vers. 2 maidens, 10 runs, and 7 wickets. On the other side, a youth named J. W. Larkin bowled uncommonly well, taking seven wickets for 39 runs. The scores were—Spencer, 29; Lausanne, 113. The match between Notts and the Australians on the 17th inst is causing much excitement in the champion cricket county. The executive of the Notts Club met en Saturday night for the purpose of selecting their team, and the following were chosen : A. Shrewsbury, W. Scotton A. Shaw, W. Attewell, F. Shacklock, W. Gunn, W. Barnes, W. Flowers, M. Sherwin, Walter Wright, and Bean or Selby.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board con- taining a report of one of their lunacy inspector's visit to the Workhouse. The report was favourable, the inspector ex- pressing his opinion that the lunatics at the Workhouse were properly cared for. He also suggested the provision of a musical box and illustrated papers.—Mr. BHOWN Said they had been pretty well provided with illustrated papers by people in the town.

TACCINTATIOIT. : The CLERK said the following was a copy of the letter sent to the Local Government Board by Mr. Ilulford, vaccination (Beer, Warrington, in reply to their communication read at the previous meeting, viz. :—" I have bad the honour to receive an extract from a letter received by the Warrington Board of Guardians from your honourable Board commenting upon the way in which I have performed my duties as vaccination officer for the Warrington and Latchford districts, and to which I most renectfully beg to offer an explanation raF requested. (I) As to my periodical returns I beg to say I have filled them up to the best of my ability those children who have been returned as vaccinated, and who, when the medical inspec- tor was here, I had written " vacc." in number 12 of my birth registers. I certainly had not received the certificates, although satisfied they had been successfully vaccinated and for which, by the request of the medical inspector, I have since received the certificates. (2) With regard to post- ponements by medical certificate, I beg to say that I have had some renewed, others I have paid personal visits and seen the children have been in an unfit state. But these cases in

future shall receive my careful and immediate attention. (3) With respect tc notices being sent to persons in default at the expiration of three months, I respectfully beg to say that I have paid them personal visits, thinking they would have more effect than sending notices. 1 may say that I have sent every defaulter a notice—in many cases they have bad the " A " and " B " notioes,and responded to them in such a manner that over 600 chil- dren have been vaccinated since the medical inspector vitae here last March. I pray that the above facts may receive your favourable consideration, and most respectfully and. earnestly say that any past omissions will serve as an incen- tive to be more diligent in the future discharge of my clnties."—The CLEtax asked if it was the wish of the Boar& that they express an opinion to the Local Government Board that they were satisfied with this explanation by Mr. Holford.—The CHLIRMAN expressed himself in favour ot this suggestion, and the matter then dropped.

Public Analysts have submitted CADBURY'S COCOA to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— Advt. SENT MAD BY MOONLIGHTERS.—A tailor, named Crean, at Chit Ales, county Kerry, has been rendered insane by the excitern.nt of a visit from a gang of moonlighters last week who fired shots and threatened to boycott him if he con- tinned to work for a boycotted farmer. He has been taken to a lunatic aSpluM. THE SHOP Huns' BEGrIATION EILL —The Select Com- mittee of the House of Commons on the Shop Hours' Regulation Bill met on Monday, when petitions in favour of closing at eight o'clock on five days of the week and at ten o'clock on Saturday having been presented, the evidence was concluded, and the committee proceeded to discuss the clauses of the bill. SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDENT.—A shocking occurrence has taken place in Elm Colliery, Flintshire. A man named Thomas Edwards was working in the. pit when a heavy fall of roof took place. The deceased's head was caught against the edge of a tub he was filling, and his face cut completely away from the crown of hi* head to beneath his chin. I Death was instantaneous, the decease i's face being buried under the debris. RAT'S COMPOUNn for Coughs and 0,11,15, !s ecrWly service- able far 11,.brses and 'Cattle. div.head: PAUPERS' LEGACIES.
div.p: PAUPERS' LEGACIES.

Mr. BROAD.BENT said that a little while ago he saw from a paragraph in a newspaper that in one Union a male pau- per bad a legacy left him. He begged to remain in the workhouse, and he would contrilue the cost of his mainten- ance, but the authorities would not, or could not, allow him. to do so, and he was turnal out, but immediately spent the legacy in dissipation, and returned again to the workhouse a pauper. Mr. Broadbent then asked the clerk if it would not bare been legal to agow that man to stay in the workhouse?—The CLERK : I think not.—Mr. Bnows thought a claim for the man's maintenance during a year or two should hare been made, and that would have lessenel his legacy.—The CLERK mentioned that in that Union they generally made a claim for, at all events, one year's maintenance in similar cases.—The subject then dropped, and the relief cases were proceeded with..

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, MAY 15, 1886.

THE HOME RULE BILL of the Govern- ment may be said, so far as Parliament is con- cerned, to lie trembling in the balance; but with the country it outweighs everything that can be urged against it—in other words the people are heartily in its favour. Last week the General Council of the Warrington Liberal Association passed a resolution in favour of Mr. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule scheme, and on Monday evening the Three Hundred of the Newton Division gave their support to the measure, and expressed their unabated confidence in the Prime Minister. These are but samples of the rest; and if it be true that what Lancashire thinks to-day England will think to-morrow, there need be no doubt as to the ultimate success of the Home Rule policy. It may, however, be said that the people are by no means the best judges of the details of a measure which is admittedly complicated, and which deals with problems which tax the best intellects of the day. This may be granted; but the issue just now, as Mr. GLADSTONE is careful to explain, is not as to details, but as to whether legislative autonomy shall be granted to Ireland-- whether the time has arrived for giving ' Irishmen an opportunity of managing their own affairs in their own way. As to this. issue, the people of this country, so far as they have spoken, have expressed themselves with emphasis. Those present at the meet- ing on Monday evening cheered Mr. Join; CROSFIELD, the Liberal candidate for Warring- ton, when he said they were in favour of justice being done to Ireland; and they were equally enthusiastic when he said he would support Mr. GLADSTONE in this matter through thick and thin. Warrington is, of course, but one town amongst many; but it is not to be forgotten on the other hand that Lord HARTINGTON'S constituents withheld from hirn an expression of confidence when he appealed to them; that when Mr. GOSCHEN went to Leeds a large out-door gathering demonstra- ted'against him; and that the National Liberal Federation, which ha S great regard for Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, declined to adopt his view, and committed itself to the support of the Govern- ment. The fact is the people, unlike some of their representatives, have faiql, and they have trust; they have faith in Mr. GLAD- STONE'S statesmanship, and they can trust the Irish people. Lord HARTINGTON, as leader of the opposition to the Home Rule Bill, haS-
IIL4H

I°r 11 Pent lost faith, and he is not dis- Posed to take anything upon trust. It is hard r Liberals, who have a well-founded and 2,lnoere admiration for his lordship, to see ,Pina incurring the grave responsibility which Ile took upon himself on Monday evening, in Moving the rejection of•the Government Bill; but he is not to be blamed--he is rather to be temmended—for following the dictates of his C.onscience. We have too many politicians I,rl the House of Commons who will do noth- ing till, as the phrase is, they see how the at Jumps. A HARTINGTON, whether he sit the Liberal or on the Tory side of the Ouse, is worth a score of these waiters upon Providence. And having said this much, let ask the question—What is the basis of .ierd HARTINGTON'S opposition to the Home scheme?le The answer, to put it in r D.lef; is—distrust of the Irish people. He gives his reasons for this distrust, and it is as !fell to remember that portions of Irish history nave been "burnt in" by the loss of a bz other 'who was murdered on Irish soil at the very inoment that he held in his hand a message °f Peace to Ireland. Lord HARTINGTON does allude in his speeches to this terrible lirl.agedy, but can we wonder—can we blame 1111—if it has its influence in leading, him ;(2$ conclude that the people of Ireland are not '0 be trusted with the exercise of the large kreers of administration and legislation which r. GLADSTONE would confer upon them ? t is but fair to say that his lordship gives reasons for urging that the °Tne Rule Bill—as it stands—is opposed • Liberal doctrines and Liberal principles. 41e observed on Monday night that if it ere proposed to extend this measure to ?cotland, the people of Scotland would scout • but what of that? The question is—is acceptable to the people of Ireland? Much, apti. ost everything, turns on the response to t °ls question, and we are glad to find that the ainswer is emphatically in the affirmative. -Lord HARTINGTON (as well as Mr. CHAMBER- LA/N) thinks it a blot on the bill that it does 11°t provide for the retention of the Irish Illernbers at Westminster; but this is a debate- 111°,1e point, approach it as we may; and if the (Irish leaders urge, as they do urge, that they b° not wish to be directly represented in two athaments, the matter is one, surely, in which NZ should have some regard to Irish opinion. "e must confess that, looking back at the Part that members for Ireland have for some I litie played in th- Britisn Theatre, we should Irt be at all sorry to see them, with bag and a. ggage, en route for Dublin to play a new PI"; in a new Irish Theatre, with the pros- Peet of "a tremendous long run." What lyould certainly be ha' eful, and what English- ten would not long tolerate, would be an rangement by which the representatives of Ireland should be in a position not only to ,eg!slate for themselves, but to determine the legislation of England by trooping back to St- Stephens, whenever they thought fit, to turn out the Government of the day. Let ' Ireland by all means have freedom to govern herself but when it comes to a question of , freedom to govern England also, we must stand on our own defence and cry " Hands • The question, it will be seen, has two si▪ des, and we are inclined to think with Mr. D. AVITT and Mr. T. P. O'CONNOR that, for a time, at any rate, Irishmen will have enough to do. in a Parliament of their own without troubling themselves as to what is going on tit. Westminster. "Hereafter," as Mr. W. 0 ERTEN said in the House of Commons on I nday night, "when a happier spirit pre- !ailed, they might desire the participation of Irishmen in the government of the Empire, and he believed they would find them a source 4f greater strength than when they were de- tained against their will." There are, unfor- t,nriately, those who would have us disbelieve tne Irish in the statements they make on this • in other features of the Home Rule Scheme: but we are not amongst those who v!ould say, in haste, that all Irishmen are liars, and repent of the statement at leisure. Referring to Lord SPENCER, Mr. O'BRIEN generously said : Tile Mistakes that he made belonged to the system, 44,c1 the manliness with which he had acknowledged , ra belonged altogether to himself. One touch of Alndliness, one speech at Newcastle had obliterated tet!rs of bitter memories; and the speech of the Plr.ae Minister a few weeks ago, of kindly English Teling inside and outside the House, had done more • an fifty coercion acts to bring about a real union nIE the two countries. Are we to conclude that the member for South Tyrone was shamming when he gave vent to this manly and eloquent expression of sentiment—that he was making a mockery of What is best in human nature? If the Irish Problem is ever solved it will not be with a sense of distrust as the prevailing feeling. will rather be by acting in the belief that hke begets like; that trust begets trust ; and that if we sow the seeds of kindness we may 'lope to reap a kindly harvest.

GREECE has at last been brought to see— but not before being humiliated by a blockade ----that if she insisted on fighting she would have to reckon not only with Turkey, but with the great European Powers. She has been for some been armed to the teeth and ready to fly at the throat of Turkey. It was con- ended, and with some show of reason, that if a change was made in the Berlin Treaty in the interests of Bulgaria, it should be made, too, in the interests of Greece. It seemed for a time in vain to urge that PRINCE ALEXANDER had had to submit to the will of the signatory Powers. and tin. t Greece could hot be allowed to invade Turkey with a view to extending her frontier. The Greeks con- tinued to arm, and to disregaid the advice even of such a warm friend as Mr. GLAD- STONE, until, as it seemed, there was no- thing for it but to present an ultimatum 4nd blookade her ports. The French Pleni- Potentiary at Athens continued. to plead With the Greek Government, but at the eleventh hour the Greek Premier showed himself stubborn, and preferred to resign rather than submit. The Greeks may think !Ike), are a match for the Turks-; but they are not such fools in their own Conceit as to supposl they are capable struggling against the forces of United -F.urope. They have been wise, and wise In time to save themselves, and make their protest effective. The hour will come When their claim to an extended frontier will be recognised; but meantime they must 'wait. To go to war at the present moment to secure their ends would be to court failure, and make their attainment im- Dossible for many years—perhaps for a generation. Turkey as the Sick Man 1,5 not yet incapable of striking a blow; unt even if he were helpless there are too many interested parties awaiting the dissolution to allow Greece to have her own v'ay in the matter. The concert of Europe has in this case been a great advantage; it has prevented a war which might have de- veloped into a conflict of great magnitude. n view of a result so satisfactory, the remark ls obvious that if the BEACONSFIELD Govern-

div.head: FRODSHAM WATER SCHEME.
div.p: FRODSHAM WATER SCHEME.

At the meeting of Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority on Tuesday. the minutes of the Frodskane Parochial Commit- tee were read, containing a report en the water scheme from Mr. Bancroft, the engineer. After remarking upon a section submitted to the Local Government Board inspector, he alluded to tbe suggested plan of extending the No. 1 bore- hole. and said the additional depth of boring required the inspector estimated would be about 200 feet, it was already 102 feet below the surface; and he further considered it probable that the water would rise in the borehole to nearly the bottom of No. 1 well. He quite coincided in the opin- ion that if the borehole was extended to the depth suggested an ample supply of water could be obtained, but he very much doubted if the water would rise in the borehole at all times to within many yards of the bottom of the well (and without it did a gravitation scheme could not be carried out, in consequence of the deep cutting necessary in the highway at 1' ive Crosses). He had been most anxious to carry out a gravitation scheme, and thus save , the cost of pumping, but without Parliamentary powers were obtained to enable them to acquire the water rights, he failed to see that any local gravitetion scheme could be carried out. It had been suggested tbat water might be obtained from the Liverpool Corporation's new Welsh scheme, but if 60,000 gallons per day were required it would I caet (at 6d per 1,000 gallons, the price the Corporation was offering to cell it in bulk, and at 25 years' purchase) £13,687 10a. That would be exclusive of a cost of a meter, meter- house, and the piping to the Corporation aqueduct; in fact: the value of the water only. He had under the circumstan- ces carefully considered tee question of obtaining a supply from other sources. There were two places where boreholes might be sunk, viz., in the old gravel pit near the fault at the west of Such Pant, and on Mrs. Hebbert's laza in Flain-lane. He explained the formation of eech spot, and advised them to have Mrs. Ilebbert's land first tested, and if an ample sneply of good water could be obtained, it would be a much cheaper scheme at the onset, and the working expenses hereafter would be much less than the one at Five Cro.lies. He had not bad

time to go thoroughly into the scheme and its probable cost, but should the water rise within a reasonable level in the borehole he thought the cost of pumping could be re- duced to a minimum. The scheme would not provide for supplying a few houses above the level of the reservoir and the property in the lordship with water ; but if it was con- sidered necessary that all the property in the township should he provided for, a small water tower. 50 feet high, might be built adjoining the reservoir, and the water lifted nib) it. Should the scheme be required to embrace the lordship, a rising main would have to be laid up Fluin-lane and another reservoir constructed on the high land above the village of Overton. The average price for sinking a bore- hole per foot run for the first 100 feet is 9e 6d, and for the second 100 feet 12s ed. The casing would be about 10a per foot extra. This would be exclusive of the cost of pumping to teat the yield. The committee discussed the report at considerable length, and it was decided to obtain accounts of all liabilities in connection with the late schemes, and the clerk was directed to forward a copy of Mr. Bancroft's report to each member of the committees for consideration previous to the next meeting, when the matter would be further considered.

PROPOSED COUNTY COURT FOR WIDNES. EXPECTED ESTABLISHMENT. On Thursday morning a meeting of tradesmen and other gentlemen interested in the establishment of a county court for Widnes was held in the dining-room of the Central Hotel. Mr. James White occupied the chair, and amongst those present were Messrs. R. Lewis, R. Booth, J. Beach, J. W. Knowles, S. Owens, T. J. Peters, A. Parkes, J. Fitzpat- rick, and %V. T. Husband. The Chairman said that at previous meetings the abso- lute necessity of having separate county court sittings bad been clearly proved. The great inconvenience and expense of going to St. Helens bad been pointed out, and the hard- ship caused to many poor people had beer. set before the public. Since the last meeting Mr. Husband, the deptity coroner, had been indefatigable in the matter. He then called upen it Mr. Husband, who read a number of communications he tied had with Mr. Edwards Moss on the subject. Mr. K. Muir M'Kenzie, the secretaiy to the Lord Chancellor had written to Mr. Moss, and said that the case for a county court at Widnes was very strong from his (Mr. Moss's) view, and unless the judge of the district had a very strong opinion to the contrary, he (Mr. 111‘Kenzie) had little doubt the Lord Chancellor would meet the wishes of the Widnes people. Mr. Moss also wrote that he had seen his Honour Judge Thompson, and he was glad to say that he had kindly consented not to offer any further opposition to the petition to hold a county court in Widnes, provided he was not ex- pected to continue to attend as many sittings at St. Helens as he had to do under present circumtrances. Mr. Moss had communicated these views of Judge Thompson to Mr. Muir M'Kenz;e, and urged that the matter should be pressed for- ward. Mr. Husband said if they could urge Mr. Moss to further exertions, and if they could give him some reason for again approaching the Lord Chancellor, they were within a measurable distance of getting what they wanted. (Hear, hear) The Chairman thought their position was now very satisfactory, and it would be a pity to let the matter drop.

IN'ir J. Beach moved—"Thlt this meeting convey to Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P. for the Widnes division of Lan- c ishire, a hearty vote of thanks for the energy and tact that he has displayed in the matter of the petition entrusted to

I ment had taken a similar course with regard to Turkey, Europe might have been spared the ravages and horrors of the war between Turkey and Russia. The great Powers of Europe were then practically agreed as to the demands to be made upon "the unspeakable Turk ; " but when it came to a question of do- ing what is now bcing done with Greece —namely, enforcing the demand—the Eng- lish Government backed out; concerted action came to an end, and a war commenced which resulted in Turkey being utterly de- feated and demoralised. Lord BEACONSFIELD in that matter posed as the friend of Turkey; but Droved to be her worst enemy. In the same way, if Mr. GLADSTONE had encouraged Greece by declining to act with the other European Powers, Greece would have rushed to war, and possibly to her own destruction. The Tories talk about a "spirited foreign policy ;" but they leave it to a Liberal states man to carry it out,

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

"What a splendid show !" exclaimed a spectator as he waited at Liverpool, on Wed nesday, to see the Queen. " Show of what ?" queried his eripping companion. "Show of umbrellas, to be sure," responded the wag And so it was Tradesmen little thought, when they were fixing up their " bits of bunt- ing," that other bunting would be run up which would shut theirs from view.

"Queen's weather" has passed into a proverb in association with her Majesty ; and there are people who had begun to think there was " something in it ; " so Jupiter Pluvius poured down the rain incessantly, and in tor- rents, on the occasion of the Royal visit—just to show that he was master of the situation and no respecter of persons.

But the Queen was equal to the occa- sion. She is a great stickler for form and ceremony, and doing one's duty; and she set an example, on Wednesday, which de- lighted her loyal subjects. It was a matter of form—the weather being fine—that she should appear in an open carriage; but, if it was permissible for the Duke of Cam- bridge to review troops with an umbrella over him, it was felt that her Majesty would be justified, considering the stormy weather, in making use of a closed carriage. But she did not; she allowed herself to be seen, and when the vast crowd which lined the principal streets observed that her Ma- jesty was in an open carriage, the cheers which rent the air showed how highly the populace appreciated the noble self-sacrifice of the Queen. Happy people in having such a Queen, and happy Queen in having such a people!

But it is a nice point, after all, whether, where so much depends on the health and life of a Sovereign, such a risk should be run. A Court of her Majesty's judges—if the point were submitted to them—would probably decide in favour of a closed car- riage—particularly if there was any uncertainty as to the succession. But they were not con- sulted ; England's Queen did what she be- lieved to be her duty, and the hearts of her people warmed towards her Majesty—even through their wet clothes.

And some of them were wet. Volunteers and others who were on duty for hours, in the rain, were wet to the skin. Some fared worse than others—just as commanding officers had, or had not, regard for their men. A number of the Warrington Volunteers have been heard to complain that they were badly used in being put off with a pie and a glass of beer. Perhaps some of them went to Liver- pool under the impression that they were going to dine with the Queen? Or can it be that Colonel Greenall thought from the look of his men that they had had enough, for one day, of "heavy wet?"

Sir Gilbert Greenall has at last achieved distinction ; and the Tories, proud of the fact, floated a flag above the club on Tuesday, for on Tuesday the member for Warrington "attained his Both birthday." It is rather hard on "the odd, old fellow" that his nose should be kept to the political grindstone at his time of life—not that he does much; still, it is rather hard, so the Liberals intend to relieve him of his post at the next elec- tion. -- • Major Sanderson, speaking on behalf of the Loyalists, says their " unalterable deter- mination" is to resist Home Rule "if neces- sary by force of arms." There is great vir- tue of course in an "if," and it may not be thought " necessary " to fight, even if the Home Rule Bill be passed. But why do these people, Lord Randolph Churchill in- cluded, prate about loyalty, at the very mo- ment that they are talking fustian about taking up arms against the Crown? But the Home Rule Bill will not pass—just yet. Yesterday Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain and their following met and combined to ensure its overthrow • and they seem to be confident of success. They were very careful to say that they were not called upon to bring forward any alternative mea- sure. But if they defeat the bill—what then? They can't go on for ever " beating time." Certain of the Whigs, Tories, and Radicals may agree about turning the Government out, but they will not agree about anything else. 'Tis not their nature to.

From a return just issued, it appears that the Prescot Board of Guardians. with a daily average of .44.1 inmates, spend over £2O a year in intoxicating liquors. About L's of the total goes for " spirits." The clerk says the return will compare favourably with those of other Boards. possibly, but what if the result of the whole expenditure should be un- favourable? Is it not time that this ques- tion were considered, not by the Prescot Board only, but by every Board? Who could have thought it? At a public meeting at St. Helens, on Monday, held in connection with the Liverpool District of the Wesleyan Methodists. in furtherance of the temperance cause, it was stated that there was not a temperance society amongst the Wesleyans at St. Helens. The Wes- leyans cannot of course be proud of that fact. But they are going to take away the reproach; they are forming a temperance so- iety which, it is to be hoped, will try to , fetch up for lost time."

Now that the inhabitants of the Widnes district have got an M.P. to themselves, it is quite natural that they should want a County Court of their own. It is certainly a hard- ship that they should have to go to St. Helens. When the matter in dispute be- tween Brown and Jones is one of five shil- lings, or less, it is obvious that five shillings or more may be spent in loss of time in get- ting torthe Court.

div.head: , THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 15, 1886.
div.p: , THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 15, 1886.
LOCAL NEWS.

PRODSHAM PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE —Mr. A. Thomas, J.P , haa been for unanimously re-elected chairman of this committee. WIDNES WESLEYAN SOCIETY. The Rev. James Bry- ant, of Cnorley, has accept an invitation to labour in Wid- res after the next Conference, consequent upon the re- moval of the Rev. JAS. liothersell to Manchester. COLONIAL AND CONTINENTAL CHURCH SOCIETY.—In aid of this society, a sermon was on Sunday morning, in St. Mary's Church, Widnes, and in the evening in St. Paul's Church, Widnes, preached by the Rev. A. R. M. Finlayson. There were good congregations. Sores OF TEMPERANCE, WIDNES.—Under the auspices of this 'society an entertainment was given in Malin'e temper- ance Hall, on Saturday evening, to a good auellence. Mr. T. S Swale presided. An admirable programme was gone through, Miss Travis officieting as accompanist. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—On Monday afternoon, while Mr. Luke Hargreaves, son of Mr. James Hargreaves, inventor of the celebrated Hargreaves and Robinson procese,Was atten- ding some machinery at the works in Ditton-road, he had the whole of the fingers of the left hand completely cut off. He was at once tattera to Dr. Niel's surgery, and the injuries attended to. A GALLANT WIDNES RAILWAY PORTER.—A few months ago Joseph Whalley, e porter at tile Central Station, Widnes, risked his life in recuing a lady from the front of a train at that station. Yestei day Mr. Meldruni, general manager of the line, handed to Whalley, at the .Central Station, Liverpool, a beautiful silver ne,clat and an address from the Royal Humane Society as a reward for his bravery. . UNITED METHODIST FREE CHLIRCK, WlDNES.—Special services were held di this place of worship on Sunday, when the Rev. J. W. Chisholm, of Liverpool, occupied the pulpit. On Monday evening the rev. gentleman delivered a lecture on Billy Bray" at the same place. Mr. Clarke. of Ditton, presided, and there was a good attendance. Col- lections were made. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY .c.:ClIOOL RUNCORN.— On Sunday the anniversary services were held, and the Revs. J. Causland and D. Schofield occupied the pulpit, the former in the in truing and evening, and the latter in the afternoon. Specially se!ected hymns were sung by the scholars at each service. The collections in aid of the school funds amounted to £lB 3s. Specter. SERMONS AT WIDNES.—At Milton Congrega- gational Chapel on Sunday evening the Rev. R. G. Hughes continued his addresses • to working-men and their wives. His subject was "An hour with the ants." On Sunday morn- ing and evening the Rev. R. Yeatman preached special ser- mons, the titles of his discourses being "Zeal in religion " and " The nature and necessity of regeneration." BUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meetieg was held at Dutton Workhouse. Lieut.-Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present the Rev. J. Lock- wood. Messrs. W. Farrell, W. Fisher. S. Taylor, E. Aaron, Lewis, Hall, Whitley, H. Percival, Hamilton, Wallington, Hadfield, Brandreth, J. Stokes, H. Linaker (clear), and W. Linaker (deputy clerk). There was no business of Pub- lic interest. SINGULAR ACCIDENT AT WIDNES —When James Tobin, a man employed at the Widnes works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, was examining a still at the works on Tuesday morning, an explosion of the gas therein took place and the man's head, face, and neck was badly 'burned. Scarcely a hair was left upon that part of his body. He was taken to the accident hospital, where every attention was paid to him. TEMPERANCE LECTURE AT WIDNES.—Mr, J. Nichols, the American temperance orator, has paid a visit to Widnes On Sunday afternoon last he was present at a service in Mali's Temperance Hall, conducted by Mr. F. Lawrinson, and also in the evening, when Mr. W. alibos conducted a service. On Monday evening Mr. Nichols deliver. d one of his popular lectures, entitled "Home v. Public-houses." The,e was a moderate attendance, and Mr. H. Brunner pre- sided. LOCAL GENTLEMEN AT THE LIVERPOOL CORPORATION BANQUET.—Amongst those who were invited to attend the banquet given by the Mayor and Corporation of Liverpool, on Tuesday evening, to their Royal Elighneases the Duke of Connaught, K.G., sod Prince H,nry of Battenburg, on the occasion of her Majesty's visit, were Sir Thomas Edwards-Moss, Bart., Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., Mr. E. K. Mu?pratt, Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, and Mr. Thomas Mathi,son. BUNCORN AND WIDNES AND TIIE QUEEN'S VlSlT.—Wed- nescliy, when the Queen held her state Procesiou through the thoroughfares of the city of Liverpool. was observed as a holiday by the tradesmen and others in Widnes and Run- corn, and the railway traffic was very heavy. Trains were much delayed in consequence, but there was an absence of accidents. Owing to the lateness of the trains persons who expected to reach home by midnight did not arrive until two o'clock on Thursday morning. STRIKE AT THE TSARS'S COPPER WORKS, WIDNES. There came into force yesterday at these works a notice reducing the wages of one half of the men employed there, by about 101 per cent, or 4e 3cl per week. The men's wages were to be as follows :-5s fid per charge, 13 charges; charge-pickers and tankmen, is 91 per charge for picking up and Is 10 for emptying. Great dissatisfaction prevails amongst the men at these terms, and on Thursday evening they held a meeting to discuss the situation. They agreed to accept a reduction of 5 per cent but the manager of the works said the directors had decided not to give way in the least, and ordered the men to draw the furnaces empty. This was done, and about 100 men then went on strike. Rl:remoter; POUCH COURT.—Yesterday, Ellen Cohen, of Mill-brow, was brought up unier a warrant charged with assaulting Mary Naughton. The parties are neighbours, and through some unexplained cause a quarrel had arisen between them. The plaintiff alleged that she dare not go out of the house in consequence of the threats of the prisoner. When she did, however, venture out on Saturday, the prisoner pulled her hair, tore her shawl, and struck her several times. The prisoner, who had pleaded guilty, alleged that Cohen made a disturbance at her house door. In default of paying a fine of 101 and costs, the prisoner went to gaol for 14 days' hard labour.—Mary Jane Ann Galla- gher, who made her 37th appearence, was sent to gaol for 14 days' hard labour in default of paying a fine of 10s and costs for being drunk and incapable in King•street. RureConN RIFLE CLUB (2ND C.R.V.) The first club competition took place on Saturday, Queen's ranges and Boor ing. The following are a few of the best scores :- 200 500 600 To- yds yde yds Cal. Lieutenant A Timmins Ordour-flergesnt Inst. W H Player 3l 33 24 88 Private Peer Davits Lance-Sergeant J itusbton Coloor-Rergfant J Mort 29 30 24 83 Corporal Dan Edwards 2B 28 24 80 Private Wm. Holt Private J,e. Dobson Sergeant Dan Clarke 24 110 18 72 Lieutenant T B Ashton Private Wm. Cooper Corporal G B Joyson Private Geo. Littlernore

SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES —Ellen Unsworth, 18 years of age, daughter of Mr. Edward Unsworth, of Farnworth, died suddenly on Tuesday aliening while in a fit. She bad been subject to fits for some time, and the doctor gave a certificate.—Patrick Baines, 10 years of age, son of a labourer living at 10, Caroline-steeet, Widnes, died on Wed- nesday evening after a brief illness. An inquest on the body of the boy was opened yesterday afternoon at the Court House by Mr Brighouse, county coroner. It appeared that the deceased had retired to rest in good bealth on the previous night, and during the night complained of being unwell, and in tbe afternoon died. His stepmother deposed that she did not call in a doctor because she did not think he was so ill. She had not been in the room where the de- ceased slept for three weeks. He was insured for £5. The Inquest was adjourned until Monday to permit of a post mortem examination being made. PRESENTATION AT BUNcOnIL—On Tuesday night the members of the Runcorn Parish Church Glee Class met in the National School, for the purpose of making a presenta- tion to their conductor, Mr. J. Warbani. Mr. Jordan occu- pied the chair. The class formed in tbe early part of the winter, bad a very successful season under Mr. Warham's guidance, and the members desiring to testify their appre- ciation of his services, offered him through Ms. G. Moss, a handsome writing desk. Mr. Moss, in making the presenta- tion said that Mr. Warham had conducted the class with conspicuous ability and bad shown an urbanity and a genial disposition that had won the regard and esteem of all those who had come in contact with him.—Mr. Jordan made a few remarks eulogistic of Mr. Warbam'a disposition and services, and then the recipient responded. After thanking the members for their gift, he expressed the hoped that that etlis would continue in future, and that they would meet with even greater success next year than they had in the past—Another presentation also took place Masters Mellor, Hampson, Houghton. and Clark, who bad assisted in the recent performance of the cantata, 'Daughter of Jairas," were each given a copy of "Hymns Antrient and Modern." ItuNCOEN INDUSTRIAL BUILDING SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of this society was held in the National School on Monday night, Mr. A. Jordan, chairman of directors, pre- sided. Mr. J. E. Meredith, secretary, read the annual re- port, which stated that at the close of the first year of the existence of the society 119 books bad been issuad, contain- ing 262 shares and representing the sum of £26,200. One appropriation by ballot and one by sale had been made. The former was won by Mr. Edward Newton, to whom the sum of £2OO had been advanced. The appropriation by sale was purchased by Mr. James Goodwell, at a premium of £6O lOs for two shares, which in regard to the financial position of the society mast be taken into consideration. The directors, taking into account the recent great depression of trade in Runcorn, congratulated the members on the success of the first year, but poiated out that it would be for the benefit of the society if each member would exert himself t') introduce his friends, so that all the shares might be taken up as speedily as possible. The balance sheet showed that the total income had been £313 15s 93, which included the sum of £287 3s 6,1 for members' subscriptions. The expenditure included £59 9.3 for formation expenses, £25 for secretary's salary, £l6 2i for directors' fees, and £5 10s for rent of office. The capital account showed a balance in favour of the society of £57 Os Bd. The certificate of Messrs. C. R. H. Harrison and W. H. Rogerson, auditors, was appended to the report.—On the motion of Mr. E. Newton, seconded by Mr. Burrows, the report and balance sheet was adopted after a number of questions had been satisfactorily answerad. Tne retiring directors, Messrs. A. Jordan, J. K. Digges, Wm. . Sotto°, and E. unison, were re-elected, and the auditors, Messrs. C. R. H. Harrison and W. H. Rogerson, were also re-appoiated.

NEW POSTMASTER FoR Win/MS.—Mr. J. Payne. chief clerk of the Boat Office, Warrington, has been appointed postmaster at Widnes ibi.plac,e of Mr. Dannett, promoted to St. Helene about nine months ago. Mr. Payne has been engaged in the Warrington Mlle- for about twenty years. PRIMITIVE NltertluDlSti AT WIDNES.—The anniversary of Simile; Cross Pf M-thodist t;hapel eras celebrated on Sunday, when the Rev. F. N. Shimmio, Earlestown, preached to good congregations. In the afternoon 'lr. i. Rollason delivered an address to the teachers, scholars, and friends. Collections w.re made in aid of the funds. STEALING COAL AT lAUNCOaN.—At Runcorn Court on monday, Mary Ann Dorman. aged 15, was charged with stealing 14 be. of coal, value id., the property if the Bridge- water Navigation Compauy. P.C. Volts proved seeing the girl take the coal from the company's coal yard at Top Locke. The girl, who denied being in the yard, but ad- mitted taking coal from "just outside," WAR fined ss. STEALING A PINT OF BEER AT RUNCORN.— Mary Ann Burns and Mary Ann Linney, young •women, were charged with stealing a pint of beer. value 2id, front the Fleetwood Arms, Chutch-street, kept by Joseph Oates. On Sunday evening the women went into the vaults and asked for a pint of ale on trust. Their request waa refused, and then they asked for a pint in the ordinary vay. Upon tine liquor being put into a can. Burns ran away with it and the other prisoner followed. They were each sentenced to seven days' bard labour. THE HOURS OF MARRIAGE.—The Hours of Mar- riage Bill has received the. Royal Assent, and becomes operative at once. Marriages may, there- fore, now take place between eight and three o'clock, whether in places of worship or at regis- trars' offices. .

ILLNESS OF Mn. EDWIN WAUGH.—MT. Edwin Waugh, the Lancashire author, who is now in his TOth year, has just undergone a dangerous operation for the removal of cancer from the tongue. The operation was successfully performed by Dr. Samuel Buckley. The patient is now lying at the Knows- ley Hotel, Cheetham lull Road, Manchester, in the care of Dr. Buckley and other medical friends, and it is understood he is making sa;isfactory pro- gress. -

A BICYCLIST SUMMONED.—A respectably-dressed young man named Cl.arles Latham was summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday for riding a bicycle on the footpath at Winwick on the Ist May. Defendant, who pleaded not guilty, was defended by Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens.— P.C. Parker deposed that he saw the defendant riding a bicycle on the footpath, and watched him for about 40 yards. Defendant then dismounted, and ran his bicycle on the road: In reply to Mr. Swift, the officer said the defendant was riding his bicycle between 300 and 400 yards from where be (witness) saw him.—The magistrates considered there was a doubt in the case, and dismissed it. They did not blame the officer for his zeal in the matter.

THE SHIP CANAL.-- Many persons who have in the course of the last three or four weeks passed along Knutsford-road may have noticed,with in thirty or forty yards of the railway crossing at Latchford, a few workmen engaged in excavating a shaft of not very large dimensions, without for a moment suspecting that these workmen were the advance guard. so to speak, of the great army of navvies and other toilers who may—if the Manchester Ship Canal scheme escape the dangers of a dilatory legis- lature and the many other perils to which so enor- mous an undertaking is subject—in a short time invade the locality. Yet so it is, though of course this is not really a commencement with the prac- tical work of constructing the canal, but rather a preliminary test to ascertain the nature of the work that will have to be undertaken in this locality. It , was, we believe, Mr. Leader Williams, the eminent engineer of the ship canal scheme himself, who said that the making of the great waterway did not de- pend so much upon the engineer, whose work was comparatively simple, as upon the financiers who supplied the capital and the woikmen who supplied the labour. The main requisites would be down- right digging and excavating. It would seen from the present test that in this locality at all events those engaged in excavating would not encounter any very serious obstacles. The shaft has already been sunk to a considerable depth, the soil so far being of a light and porous character. The main impediment is a too great abundance of water, and were it not for almost continual pumping the shaft would apparently soon be flooded. But this diffi- culty would of course not be so much felt in a con- tinuous cutting such as a canal as in a confined shaft. The soil is raised by means of a pulley and bucket, the work of digging being confined to one man. The sides of the shaft are protected with iron tubing and stone work.

him by his constituents. The committee are of opinion that by his perseverance the objects of the petition are within measurable distance of being accomplished, and they beg to urge him to further efforts to obtain her Majesty's order for the holding of a monthly court at Widnes." Mr. Beach seid Mr. Moss had been untiring in his endeavours. Before when they bad appealed to the lord Chancellor on the sub- ject they had never been received in such a favourable manner. Mr. Millar seconded the motion.

Mr R. Lewis said he should like to add a word in support of the resolution. He was glad the proposition had been proposed and seconded by gentlemen who were not. sup- posed to have any great sympathy with Mr. Edwards-Moss's political views. He had heard an independent opinion of Mr. Edwards-Moss, and that opinion had been expressed by the most Radical of the members of the House of Commons, that they considered that in Mr. Edwards-Mot:8 the Widnes division had a member of whom they oti.tht to be proud. He was looked upon as a very hard-working inembi-r ; he had ingratiated himself in all sorts of quarters in the House of Commons, and he thought the result was approved of. Mr. Beach said he had heard something similar to that. He did not give Mr. Edwards-Moss hi vote at the last election, that was certain. (Laughter.) From wbat he had heard Mr. Edwards-Moss appeared to be behind the scenes in the House of Commons. .

Mr. Lewis said he was simply trying to show that the thanks were fully deserved, and that in Mr. Edwards-Moel for this and other matters they had a very good man. Mr. Millar : As well as an ornamental one. Mr. Beach : It is a question whether I than% vote for hirn next time.

The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. Lewis then moved and Mr. Husband seconded, "That this Meeting learns with pleasure that the granting of a county court for Widnes has gained the conditional appro- val of his Honour Judge Thompson, and trusts that be will continue to regard the movement in .4 favourable light, and will give his valuable assistance in completion of the arrangemsnts." The niotiou was carried.

Mr. Knowles moved a resolution authorising Mr. Husband to forward the resolutions to the proper quarters, and ex pressing to that g.-ntlecnan the gratitude or the meeting for his assiduous efforts to obtain a County Court tor Widnes. —Mr. A. Parkes seconded the tuotien, which was adeptt:d unanimously. A vote of thanks to Mr. White for presiding concluded the proc,edings.
SCENES IN RUNCORN TA PROOMS.-A LICENSE
EN DORSED.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. Charles Reynolds, Thomas Hart, land- lord of the Three Crowns beer house, King•street, Runcern, was charged with permitting drunkennese. John Bra!Mall was charged with being drunk on licensed premises. About a quarter to eleven on the night of the Ist May Constables mith arid Barber went into the " Three Crowns." In the kitcben was the landlord standing with his back to the fire, and Brannan was sitting on a chair in a state of drunken- ness. Brannan had a glass of ale before him, and he el.:ank it in the presence of :lie constables. P.C. Smith told thi landlord that Lirennsn was drunk. The landlord de id this Warm fl tle n zte al up, but fell over a form on to the floor, and c..uld not get up without the aid of the lan lord, who led bin euts:cle the house by the shoulders. I. the Street Breenan reeled against the wall. He was very ore lake The landlord asked betide to "take no notice of it as it would be all right."—lnspector Millington deposed that Branran was drunk when he saw him in the street abut ten minutes afterwards.—Hart denied that Brannan was drunk, and said he was not served with any liquor in the house —Geo. Decide, flatman, Lymm, stated that Brannan was sober at 10-35. Hart called Dr. MacLennan, who had seen the man at ten minutes past eleven, to prove that Bran- nan was sober. The doctor, however, stated that. the tuna staggered, had a difficulty in articulating his words, and though perfect,y conscious of what be was doing and say- ing he was quite under the influence of drink.—The Bench fined Hart 40s and costs and as he had been previously con- victed during the past 12 months his license was endorsed. Brannan was tined 58 and costs 12s &I.—Wm. Treverron keeper of the Blue Ball Inn, Fryer-street, was charged with Permitting drunkenness.—Mr. IV. H. Linaker defended. At 25 minutes past ten on Saturday night, the Ist May, Con- stables Smith and Berber went into the Blue Ball Inn, and in the vaults were Felix McConn and Catheriue McConn staggering about drunk. McCoun attempted to drink a glass of beer, but he fell with his back against the wall. Catherine had also a glass of beer in her hand, and she staggered against people standing at the counter, and spilled it. The couple were curs- ing each other very violently. Police-constable Smith, in answer to Superintendent Leah, said there were 15 or 20 sailors and women of bad character in the vaults. Most of those present were more or less intoxicated, but not so badly as the McConns. The house was in a very disorderly state —Catherine McConn was called, and seid she was drunk, or she would not have been dePcing for sailors. She alleg-d that the landlord gave her a bottle of soda water to sober her so that she could go to the police station and show herself Linaker addressed the Bench for the defence, and was constantly interrupted by Catherine, who had ultimately to be removed.—Treverton deposed that be was in the parlour during the time the officers were in the house. When he went to the bit afterwards McConn and his wife were dancing an Irish jig.—Mrs. Treverton said McConn and his wife were not urunk.—Mr. Brundiit said they were sorry to see Treverton in court after so short an occupation of the Blue Ball. The Bench knew the house had a bad name. , but he as a new landlord, ought to try to make the house a better name. A fine of 20s and costs was imposed. McConn and his wife were charged with being drunk on the prem- ises, and pleaded guilty. They were each fined 103 and costs.--Felix McConn was then charged with assaulting Treverton on the 3rd lost, and Catherine McConn was charged with being quarrelsome and disorderly at the Blue Ball, and refusing to quit when requested by the landlord. It was alleged that on the afternoon of the -3rd Catherine went into the vaults and asked Trevertoa to give her a pint el ale for four oranges. He refused, and she being drunk became very noisy and quarrelsome. He put her into the street, when she seized his whiskers, and Felix McConn came up and took hold of his coat. They all three fell to the ground, and Treverton on rising discovered he bad a black eye.--Catherine, who was very noisy, claimed to have committed the assault —The Bench fined her Ss And cost', and discharged her husband.

CCOUNTS.—Ch,ques far various sums amounting to £237 Os 4d were signed. bUGGESTED NKW RAILWAY STATION AT WM/fn.—The seal of the board was attached to a petition to the London and North-Western Railway Company, asking that a rail- way station should be established on the Widnes side of Runcorn Bridge. div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board, which bad been ad- journed from Tuesday in consequence of the Queen's visit to Liverpool, was held on Thursday afternoon under the chairmanship of Mr B. Carey. Present—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Handley, Wright, Brown, W. W. Gossag«, wood, Cook, Hurband, Taylor, kieyes, Boughton. J. T. Allen (clerk), I. Carr (engineer), and Iligginsoo (surveyor.)

MIL RDWARDS•IIOB9, The Clerk read the following letter:—" House of Corn. moos, April 16, 1886. Sir,-1 received your I,Ver and the three petitions, all of wkich I presented yesterday. As ta the Borough Funds Bill. I have referred to it and at present I cannot see that any good is likely to result from its passing into law, but I don't wish to pledge myself to vote against It until I have heard it discussed at the s.cond read- ing. The other petition I shall certainly have much pleasure in eupporting. 1 applied to the Local Government Board and also to Sir E. Reed, one ot the promoters of the Public Health Act (Improvement Ex- penses) Bill on the subject of the clause you propose, and I enclose their answers. I have no doubt your petition will have a very salutary effect at the present moment, though no legislation in that direction can now be expectad until after the Easter recess.-1 am, yours faithfully, T. C. Env/Anne-Moss. Jas. T. Allen, Esq."—Under date May sth, Mr. Edwards-Moss wrote asking if the amendment to the Public Health Acts (Improvement Expenses) Bill, which the Government had consented to accept, had the approval dl the Local Board.—The Chairman said this was so far satisfactory, and they were much obliged to Mr. Moss for his attention.

A LEGACY. The Clerk reported that the executors of the late Mr. I!aac W. Robinson, formerly an oil manufacturer on the site now occupied by the Widnes Alkali Company. and who died at his residence in Liverpool about three months ago, had forwarded £lO3 to be °)aced to the hospital account of the Board. This sum ssa a legacy.—The Chairman said Mr. F. H. Gossage, the chairman, was of opinion that Mr Robinson meant the £lOO to be devoted to the Accident Hospital, but they were not asked to decide that question that day. He proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Robinson's representatives for the donation.—Mr. Heyea seconded, and lit was carried.

A NUISANCE TO CHURCH PEOPLE. Mr. F. Neil, vicar's warden at the parish church, wrote as follows, under date May 12th In accordance with a resolution passed at a recent meeting ef St. Mary's Parish Church council we beg most respectfully to draw your at- tention to the frequent occasions (especially on Sunday evenings) on which much annoyance is caused to those (in common with others) who attend St. Mary's by the escape of most offensive vapour from adjacent chemical works The council feel sure that if the subject of complaint come within your jurisdiction that steps will be taken for an eally abatement of the nuisance."—The communication was re- ferred to the Health Committee. FAILCRE IN WATER SUPPLY: ALTERATIONS TO STOCKS' WELL. -
The minutes of the Gas and water Committee stated that the 'mean rainfall for April had been 11131 inches, and that

the water in stock on April 28th was 7,993,461 gallons. It was recommended that tenders be advertised for for pro- posed alterations at Stock's Well estimated to cost about £2.250.—Mr. B. Brown in moving the confirmation of the minutes said the above recommendation was necessary in consequence of the failing supply of water at Stock's Well. The level of the water was not now what it was a year or two ago. Formerly the average yield of the well for a year was 329 millions of gallons, but at the present time the average yield was only about equal to about 281 millions per year. While at the same time we bad a considerable in- crease in the consumption. Toe average monthly deliveries were about 57 millions, but for the last three months the ayerage had been 64 millions per month, and had in one month reached nearly 68 millions, while their present ability to pump, with the shortened supply, from Stock's well, was only about 70 millions per month, and that entailed working every Sunday at Ketberly with both engines, a state of things which the Board should hardly allow. The engineer had made various recemmend- ations to the committee as to the manner of dealing with Stock's well, one of which was rather novel. While they had every confidence in their engineer they thought they should consult the interests of the Board and the rate- payers and be safer if they got outside opinion with refer- ence to the best means of obtaining an increased supply at Stock's well. The committee therefore Rot reports from three practical well sinkers and water engineers, and two of them and one partially in principle recommended that steps be taken on the lines that Mr. Carr first indicated. If tbe Board gave the committee power to make the alterations, there would be an increase in the value of the water peeved at Stock's well, provided the water they were able to pump was sold—an increase of £4,000. The alteration they sug- gested would very materially decrease the cost of the work at Stock's well, very nearly to the extent to cover the inter- est of the money they would have to expend. They proposed, however, to pay for the alterations out of revenue from water account.—Mr.Wright seconded the motion,which was carried.

div.head: FINANCE
div.p: FINANCE

The Finance Committee recommended that a rate of 131 in the £ be laid estimated to produce £5,317, for the six months ending September 30ch next —ln moving its adop- tion Mr. T. Handley .ficl the estimated expenditure for the least year was £10,121, and the actual. amount expended £10,068, showing that the expenditure was £53 lees than 1 the estimate, which he considered was very close. The es- timate of the Highway Committee was £4,303, and the ex- penditure £4,598, showing an expenditure over estitna,e £295; Health Committee estimate £1,143, expenditure £932, difference £211: Finance Committee estimate £4,675, expenditure £4,538, difference 137. The balance brought forward from the year 1884 85 was £495, and the two rates were estimated to produce £9,712, but actually produced £9,724, or £l2 over the estimate. The estimated expendi- (lure for the coming half-year was £5,544. They had a balance of .£l5l from last year, but a falling revenue. The gross assessment last year was in round numbets £140,000. This year, owing to the successful appeals of the various firms in the district, was only £127,000. This would make a difference in the rate of the whole , year of about Ved in the Z. In addition they have a, library rate of ld-in the £, and the public offices interest and sinking fund, making altogether about 24-d in the over and above what they had last year. The rate of 131 in the £ would produce, according to estimate, £5,468, and the'estimated expenditure was £5,544, leaving a deficiency of £76. They, however, expected a few receipts which would cover that deficiency.—Mr. Wright seconded the motion.—Mr. Taylor was much surprised to hear that the expendit:ae of the Highway Committee was over the esti- mate. The committee had tried to keep it under, and he was under (be impression that they had succeedel—The Chairman said the committee were really within their esti- mate, but through some inadvertence an account of £2OO was left from the previous year, and had to be charged in the highway account.—The motion was passed. Thera was no other business of public interest.

ARCH! DIACONAL VISITATION AT FRODSHAM. esterdav the annual visitation for tie admission of the churchwardens and sidesmen of the various churches in the neighbourhood of Frodsham, including Runcorn, was held at Frodsham Parish Church by the Rev. Chancellor Espin, who, in the course of his address to these officers, said : Chuch finance, in almost all the parishes, had worked itself out in definite shape. A few years ago, voluntary church rates were by no means uncommon, but at present there was in that centre of visitation, be believed, only one in. stance out of 48 parishes in which a voluntary church rate was collected. When these rates were in vogue there was. no doubt, in many quarters, a strong objection to frequent l collections, and much more te collections at every service. There was no doubt that the principle of the weekly offer- tory pad made great progress during the past few years. Our people had got better hold of the scriptural truth, very I much obscured in the days of church rates, that we ought to honour God in His house by offering him of our sub- stance as well as by worshipping him with prayers and praise. In some parishes, where the offertory was scanty, the deficiency was made up by pew rents or voluntary payments which it was difficult to distinguish from pew rents, inasmuch as if the payment was not made the sitting was not assigned. He would remind them that to let pews in a parish church was absolutely illeeal. The payment of rent for sittings' in a church was a thing un- known to ancient church law, and if it was legal anywhere it could only have been made so by a modern Act of Par- liament. In all other cases it was illegal. He advised the churchwardens to cultivate the offertory by (1) giving a full statement of the amount and the purpose of the collec- tion, which might be posted on the church doors; (2) by stirring appeals to the people; and (3) by encouraging a regular attendance at church. He pointed to the advance the Church bad made during the past 20 years amongst the populations of our great towns, and said that if it had not made similar progress in the rural districts it was because success had not been striven for so well and so hard. In conclusion, he pointed out that in 115 churches in the county there w as no collection for the diocesan institutions, and urged that the habit of giving to such iustitut ions (be- sidem stalling off school boards and school board rates) would cultivate the habit of giving to merely local pur- poses also. It was precisely in thos parishes where the collections for such institutions or for missionary purposes were the least frtqueut that toe collections for the clerk, the organist, and the warming of the church were also the most meagre. Let them remember that they formed part of a mighty organisation, the Catholic °bur* the general vigour of which resulting from their unselfish efforts would react in invigorating their parish also.

div.head: 'BUS ACCIDENT NEAR WIDNES TO
div.p: 'BUS ACCIDENT NEAR WIDNES TO
A WARRINGTON PARTY.

On Wednesday a party of ladies and gentlemen from Runcorn travelled from Widnes to Liverpool by road in a 'bus belonging to Mr Connor, of War- rington, in order to witness her Majesty's procession .through the streets, and view the other demonstra- tions of the honoured city. Notwithstanding the extremely unpropitious state of the atmospheric elements, the party succeeded in extracting much enjoyment from their surroundings, and had the Thepleasreteuorrnjourney w testifyinga theirscommencedloyaltto their Queen. half-past nine, and all went as "merry as a marriage bell" until Tarhock had been passed. Then the conveyance turned round a sharp curve, gave several alarming lurches, and after travelling a short distance fur- ther, ran into a ditch. The 'bus was over-turned, and the occupants were thrown somewhat violently upon each other. Mr. T. Kirkham, who oc- cupied a seat on the box, leaped into an adjoining field and escaped uninjured. Happily the occupants also escaped without injury, and were quickly extricated from the vehicle, only to find themselves up to the ankles in mud and water, with a gale of wind and rain prevailing. Their con- dition was anything but enviable, and it was not reassuring to discover that the four horses were unable to move the 'bus. The driver and his assist- ant were despatched to Widnes to fetch another vehicle, and the 'bus having been supported by props on one side, the ladies and several of the gen- tlemen returned into the conveyance, and passed two hours of waiting in a very jovial manner—wider the circumstances. Runcorn was reached at two o'clock next morning, and, wet and cold, all were glad to seek repose. It seems that the driver turned in mistake from the highway into an occupation road.

HOLIDAY AT EABLESTOWN.—Wednesiav, the day set apart for tue progress of her Majesty the Qa,en through Liverpool, was to some extent observed as a general holiday at Earlestown. Several of the places of business were closed, ad the Viaduct Waggon Works belonging Vie Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company were also stopped for the day. It is stated that the men were canvassei on the question of stopping for the day, and the result was an 1 overwhelming majority in favour of continuing at work. Uhe works, however, were stopped, as was also the estab- lishment of Messrs. T. and T. Vicars, machinists, &c. The Vulcan Iron Foundry, where the men started on full time on Monday last, was not closed, awl all the men remained at work. Not withstanding the fact that rain fell ine!.s- sintiv throughout the day, may persons left Earlestown for Liverpool.

div.head: 0 UR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: 0 UR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, TIIITRSDA Y.

The Irish Government Bill, Her Majesty's Govern- ment, and the Liberal party are at the present moment in a very critical state. Mr. Gladstone's speech of Monday night, in moving the second read- ing of the bill, led to the most remarkable effect ever witnessed in the house of Commons. Before he rose there was an impression on all the benches that he was charged with a message of conciliation that would remove Mr. Chamberlain's objections, and bring together a force that would triumphantly carry the second reading of the bill. The Conserva- tives, seeing a toothsome bone snatched from under their very nose, were gloomy and depressed. The Whigs were sunk in the depths of woe, whilst the great body of the Liberal party was full ot elation. Mr. Chamberlain in particular was in the. highest spirits. He was to come out victor in a tussle with Mr. Gladstone, even after he had wantonly aggro,- vated the conflict by his overbearing letter to Mr. Bolton. "Mr. Gladstone had climbed down," the Chamberlainites said, as they rubbed their hands and laughed.

Mr. Gladstone amazed the house, and utterly die- comfited Mr. Chamberlain by making it clear that he had no intention of making the expected. sur- render. He went some way towards meeting the objection to the exclusiOn of Irish members from Parliament, but halted far 'short of Mr. Chamber- lain's expectation. The effect has been to widen the gulf between Mr. Gladstone and a very large section of the Liberal party. -Whether it will be healed remains to be seen; but the situation is such that men's minds are projected beyond the next fortnight, and the question is what will be done should the bill be thrown out? There see ms no alternative from dissolution, and a aeneral Elec- tion would be forced at a time that would find the Liberal party grievously hampered by dissensions. There is, however, still hope that if Mr. Gladstone were to give a distinct pledge not to carry the bill further this session, but to take it up again at an autumn sitting at which all objection to details would be fully considered, there would be found sufficient Liberals voting for the second Leading to secure its passage.

There have been during the week two great gatherings of society. One was at the Foreign Office on Saturday night, when Lady Rosebery held. her first reception. Invitations were issued "To have the honour of meeting their Royal Hignesses the Prince and Princess of Wales." But this did not' comprise the full list of royalty present. There was, indeed, quite a family party in company with • the Prince and Princess as they passed through the throng in the splendid corridors of the Foreign Office. Our Prince, in his ordinary evening dress, was, in the matter of personal magnificence, utterly outdone by an Indian Prince clad in cloth of gold, with a great diamond flashing under his swarthy chin. Most of the Foreign Ministers were there, including M. Germadius,the Greek, full of fire and. fury, and denunciation of Powers who have it chiefly at heart to "pass indignity upon unhappy Greece." The Japanese Minister and his pretty little wife smiled their way through the crowd, both alas! in English dress. The Chinese Minister, on the contrary, wore with better effect the garb of his own country. The display of flowers used in decoration was extraordinary. The broad staircases on either side were flanked with rare plants. It is the duty of the Board of Works to supply flowers and plants at the Foreign Office receptions; but Lord Rosebery had liberally supplemented the official supply by contributions from Mentmore. The Prince of Wales, detained at the dinner at the Gordon Boys' Home, was late in coming, and it was well into Sunday morning before the last guest had departed. The other gathering was at Mr. Woodall's, last night in the spacious ground floor suite of Queen Anne's mansion. This annual entertainment began modestly enough, some three or four years ago. It was called then, as now, "a sandwich soiree," and was made up chiefly of members of the Savage Club. It has now grown to be an event of the social season. The scope of charac- ter represented at these meetings is illimitable. Actors, artists, journalists, authors, members of Parliament, peers, Ministers, and Royalty were all represented. The Duke of Cambridge came early and stayed late, thoroughly enjoying the rare grati- fication of a conversation in which Mr. Chamberlain spoke in hostility to Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Chamber- lain was in high spirits after the meeting at his house, and discussed the situation with his customary frankness. There were the usual contribu- tions to the entertainment of the evening by eminent singers, musicians, conjurers, and actors. But the company itself furnished an inexhaustible fund of interest. There is nothing like it in Lon- don, and only a man as universally popular as is the Surveyor General of Ordnance could get together such a motley mob of notable people. I hear of a movement on foot in Birmingham to present Mr. Schnadhorst with a substantial testi- mony of apppreciation of his services to the Liberal cause. It is proposed to raise a sum of £lO,OOO for presentation to the originator of the caucus system. Mr. Dixon has promised £5OO, whilst Mr. Chamber- lain has put his name down for £250, a limitation which has excited some comment. Mr. Chamber- lain is not wont to let others exceed him in munifi- cence on occasions like this, and certainly he of all men owes most to Mr. Schnadhorst's services. It happens just now, however, that between the two hitherto inseparable allies a little difficulty has arisen. Mr. Schnadhorst does not approve the policy Mr. Chamberlain is now pursuing and which threatens to bring the Tories in for an indefinite lease of power. This position is peculiarly galling to Mr. Chamberlain, who is constitutionally irrit- able under opposition of any kind. But lam sure that these circumstances have nothing to do with the accident that, in a movement making monetary recognition of Mr. Schnadherst's services,. Mr Chamberlain's cheque does not head the list. The position of a member of Parliament makes a man acquainted with strange coriespondents. A member sends me a letter received by him, doubt- less in common with all other members of House, from a private detective. The superhuman pre- science of this gentleman sees dissolution in the near distance. With a large independence of poli- tics he hastens to place his services at the disposal of members of the House of Commons. how assis- tance is to be rendered is a little vague. The detec- tive undertakes to " ascertain the weak and undecided districts where extra attention can be paid by your representatives and time and labour saved where not needed." "Thus preventing," he proceeds in a new and even more confusing sen- tence, "anxiety of mind independent of trouble and expense, as also in the event of charges being brought against you hereafter." This last suggestion is a little alarming, adding a new terror to Parlia- mentary candidature. The letter is in manuscript, and indicates an enormous outlay of trouble, sup- posing it has been addressed to the 670 members of the present House. It would be interesting to know how many replies leading to business the enterpris- ing detective has received. •

The second hearing of the Crawford case will ex- cel in dramatic interest its predecessor. Sir Charles Dilke will, of course, go into the witness box. But he will be preceded by a not less interesting wit- ness. I hear that Mrs. Crawford, who is now living in retirement in the South of Italy, has intimated her intention of returning to London, entering the wit- ness box, and upon oath repeating with her own lips the statement made by her husband at the last trial. All the servants, including "Fanny," will be in court, and will give sworn evidence, It is a fact little known, or at least generally ignored, that during the first trial the domestic servants at 76, Sloane-street had been subpoenad on behalf of Mr. Crawford, and were actually sitting in court whilst he gave evidence. It has never yet been explained why his counsel did not call these witnesses, upon whom it is presumed they reckoned for support of Mrs. Crawford's story. One of the most melancholy sights in London just now, especially since it has begun to rain, is the monument to Loyd Beaconsfield, near Palace-yard. Round the happily unconscious neck droops a great wreath of rotting primroses. At the base of the monument lies a heap of dingy and faded primroses in bunches, and wreaths, and boxes. Prominent in i the heap s a card advertising some man in Hong Kong, who for the second time has by a cheap ex- penditure upon a bushel of primroses thus pro- claimed the interesting fact of his existence. I forget his name ; but it is set forth in full print "The Honorable something or other." The real friends and admirers of Lord Beaconsfield view this outrage with distress, and wonder how long the authorities will permit it to exist. I suppose the explanation is that there would be a howl of indig- nation against the Government, and a flood of per- sonal abuse of Mr.:Gladstone, if some subordinate of the Board of Works pitchforked the dirty. mess out of the enclosure and restored the monument to its ordinnry condition of cleanliness and tidiness.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

SATunDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandley. NE3rEsts,—A man named Michael McLoughlan was brought up on a charge of having furiously driven two horses in Bridge-street nearly seven years ago. He ad- mitted the Gffence and having no means to pay a fine was committed to prison for fourteen days. MONDAY.—Bgore the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- _

man Davies, Councillor Greening. THEFT FROII A PAWNSHOP.—EIIen Gleeve was charged with stealing two pinafores, value 23 41, from the shop of Elizabeth Tunstail, pawnbroker, Winwick-street, on Satur- day afternoon Prisoner, who is the wife of a labouring man living in Robinson's-place, Lythgoes-lane, went to make a purchase, and took the pinafores. Thomas Buckley, and Edward Taylor, were each fined 53 and costs for drunkenness.—Charles Reynolds was fined is 64 and costs for a like offence ; and John Starkey, who made his 34th appearance, was tined 40s and •costs, or in default a month's imprisonment. ASSAULT ON THE POLlCE.—Joseph Allen, labourer, for- merly of Macclesfield, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting P.C. Middleton. On Saturday night th,. prisoner was drunk and lighting near the Bradley Hotel, Albert-road. As he Mused to go away the constable took him into custody. He struck the officer on the month with his fist, threw him to the ground, and kicked him everal times. He shouted that he had "done" 14 "hobbies" at Macclesfield and would " some in Widnes.—The prisoner, who was defended by Mr. Knowles, was ordered to pay a total fine of 153 and costs, or 21 days.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS TrXESDIY.—Bef are Mr. E. K. Muspratt and Mr. G. Pilkington. GONE TO BB MARRIED.—John Tarleton was summoned for assaulting Patrick Cane, a labourer, on the night of the 2nd May. The defendant asked ths, complainant for a penny in Waterloo-road, and because he refused to give him one, the defendant struck him on the head and face. The defendant did not appear, and Mr. Lewin said he thought he had gone to get married.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s and costs.

They were each fined 54 and costs.—Peter Ridyeard, for drunkenness at Haydock on the 24th nit., was fined 53 and costs.—A like penalty was imposed on Mary Atherton for a similar offence at Haydock on the Ist May. BIiLEACH OF THE PEAM—Phoebe Casey was summoned for creating a breach of the peace by knocking at a door and making use of bad language in Houghton-sttreet, Earlestown, on the 24th nit. e. he was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace.—Patrick Cunningham and Patrick Horton were charged with committing a breach of the pace by fighting at Earlestown on the 20th ult. Cunningham was bound over for six months, and Horton for three months.—Thomas Wilcock was summoned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting at Golborne on the 9th April. The defendant pleaded not guilty, and the Btncb, remarking there was a doubt in the case, dismissed it. THE GORDON BOYS' Ho.—The Prince of Wales pre- sided on Saturday night at the opening festival of the Gordon Boys' Home, held at the Criterion, London. The Duke of Cambridge, the Duke of Connaught, Prince Christian, Prince Louis of Battenburg, Prince Albert Vietor, and the Duke of Teck were among the guests.—rhe Prince of Wales, in proposing "Prosperity to the home," said the institution was not only doing a philanthropic work, bnt was honouring a great man. Her Majesty the Queen has given £2OO and the Prince of Wales £lOO to the fund. A la4y, who did not wish her name to be published, sent a , second donation of £5OOO, and the sum collected driring the evening was about £5,000. Accommodation for HO boys is intended. PRESENTS FOR MR. GLADSTONE AND MR. PARNELL—By one of the mail deliveries in London at the end of this or the beginning of next week two splendidly-bound albums, of beautiful design and elaborate decoration, will come from a large number of Irish-Americans—one as a presenta • sion to Mr. Gladstone and the other to Mr. Parnell. The contents of the albums, which will be precisely alike, form the mos curious feature in the present, because, instead of containieg portraits as ordinary albums generally do. each will he filled with a clipping of every leading article pub- lished in every American city of over 10,000 inhabitants on the subject of Mr. Gladstone's plan for giving Home Rule to Ireland. as well as copies of the letters written by Americ-in Coneefeismen on the same subject and published in an Irish-American journal. Victoria! thy conquests Are crowned with fruits of peace; Have knit the hearts of nations; Have bidden discord cease; For freelom, faith, and friendship Have flourished round thy Tlaronc, And class to class united, Our millions are as one. Victoria! thy triumph, The earliest, the best, Hath been the deep devotiod By all our hearts confessed. In them supreme thou reignest, And shalt till life be done, For bear? to heart united, Our millions are as one.
