TELVIETILL'erG WITHDUT TIMETS.—Vn Saturday, at the Town. Hall, before Mr. B. Hiram and Alderman J. Harrison, John !Jelly, a middle-aged man, residing,at 8, Water-street, St. Helens, was summoned for travelling from Wigan to St. Helens on the railway without a ticket,—Railway Detective Perkins stated that he saw the delendant alight from a train, from Wigan. When he got ta the collector he said ha had:not come by ?train, but that he had been waiting to see his.employer. Witness told him that he had seen him laoking out of the carriage window,, and if he did not pay he would be locked ap. The defendant then offered ekt, and said it was all the money he had, and they could take it. le was afterwards ascertained that he had plenty of money, ,and could have paid his fare if he had desired.—He was :Rued 20s and costs, or in defandlt, one month's impriaon- irnent.

± INDEPENDMIT METHODIST CONFERENCE AT LOWTOIT.— The half-yearly meeting and conference in connection.with the Independent Methodists,. of the Warrington Circuit was held in the Independent Methodist Chapel, Lowton Common, on Monday. There was a. very good attendance of delegates from the various places of worship ia the circuit. Mr. George Hindley (Leigh) was elected to preside. The principal places represented were Warrington, Earlestown, Leigh, Golborne, Lymm, Culcia.th, ctn. The principal business I was the consideration of the statistical reports from each district, which on the whale were considered very as.tisfac- tory. The following officers were appointed for the ensuing 12 months :—Mr. Henry Hindley (Leigh), pre:4;lant ; r. ' Mounfield (Warrington), vice-president; Mr. James Mort (Lymm), secretary ;, and Mr. John Critchlay (Warrington.) The Queen left Liverpool shortly after ten—o'dl-ock, on Thursday morning. The weather?, nnfortunately, was stilt wet and gusty, so that her wh,lle visit has been uncheneed bra single ray of sunshine. Notwithstanding the pouring rain and the high wind, a great arowd of people assembled at the specialistationin the exhibition grounds in order, to see her Majesty off and wish bez, God speed; A gnard,of honour of Laneashire Fnsiliers was at the station, and the rcute from Diewsbaro House by, way of Resehi-street• and Botanic..road was lined by Liver-posl volunteers. Several alterations had been made in•-the time of departure in order to suit the Queen's arrangwaents,and consequently.the pesple along bile road had to waitilonger thaa.they had at first anticipated:.

When at before ten her Majesty, seated in•a.carciage, with Princes& Beatrice, Duke.. of Connaught; and, Prince Henry of. Batteuberg, and escorted by a atirong squadron of Hussare, wheeled out of Neweaam House grounds into tile public road, loud cheers greeted her, and these followed her all the way to the station. On the platform the Mayor, the High Sheriff, and the Lard Lieutenant of Lanoashire were in attendance. The Asiliers' bitalt struck up. the National Anthem, and the troops presented armo. Her Majesty., on being handed :torn her carriage, bowed•very xraciously to all on the platform, but more especially to the Mayor, whom she assured al her perfeat satisfaction with all his-arnang,ements at Nevosham Housa,for hen- comfort, ' and of the great pleasure which her visit to Liverpool had afforded. her. She was then handed by her Highland at- tendants kito her saloon where the Primes Beatrice joined her. The Duke of Connaught and Prince Henry entered the next saloon, and the members of the suite haying taken their places in other carriages the train moved off amid hearty cheers from all aoaembled about the station.

LETTERS ,I.TtOBI THE Q3I3EN. The Mayor of Liverpool (Sir David Radcliffe), has re- ceived the following leXers, written, by command of hbr Majesty : Newsharm, Liverpool, May a 1886. Dsma. Mn. MAYon.,—I am commanded by the Queen to send you one hundred pounds, ts• be distributed as you think proper for charitable purpose ii Liverpool.—Yours. sincerely, .4i M314113C L PortsoNnr. Sir D. Radcliffe, Mayor of Liverpool. Newshaxri, Liverpool, May 13, 1886. DFAR Mn. MAYOA—The Queen, who ha,s been very moth • gratified by her visit to Liverpool 4, has commanded me to convey to you tha expression ofe her hearty thanks for the manner in which you have carried into effect all the ar- rangements during her abort residence here.

Tbe Queen witlies you to assure the inhabitants of your city that she was deeply moved by the enthusiastic recep- tion she met with yesterday from all classes of persons along the who!* line of her route through the city, and although her pleasure was. somewhat marred by the weather, her Majesty was amply compensated for her disap- pointment is this respect by the hearty welcome she met from the tbossands who !bed the route.

The Queen hopes you will make known to the police her admiration of the manner in which they performed their duties, and her Majesty's thanks to all who united in mak- ing her stay in Liverppt so agreeable to the Queen and to her children.—Believe tee,. yours very truly, HENRY F. PONSONBY. Sir David Radcliffe, Mayor of Liverpool. Immediately on arrixing at Windsor the Queen caused it to be announced in the Court Circular that she was some- what fatigued by her exertions since Sunday, but greatly gratified by the warmth of her reception in Liverpool.

Little things that tell—Little brothers and sisters. A pickpocket recently described himself as a professor of freeehand drawing. "Your baby is very fond of the bottle, Mrs. Masanner." "Yes, he takes after his pa." Why can you not tell a man's character by the hat he wears 'i—Becanse it is frequently put on. A Texan editor in trying to kill one man killed three. This proves that a man is never able to tell what he cart do until he tries. • It is a curious fact that while the names of all our ani- mals are of Saxon origin, Norman names are given to flash they yield. "Mamma," said a little girl, "what is that man doing over there in Mr. Thompson's porch? He has been sitting on the steps for two hours, and hasn't moved." "That, my child, is a house-painter he is painting Mr. Thompson's house by the day." SHOOST (—Fair widow, examining some black-dress mate- rial : But doesit fade Silkenstein : Yell, yeem, to dell you der troot, it fates a leedle; but it shooet goes off into a lay violet after six monts or so—ahoost lets you down mit your mourning easy and natural. Little Randolph one day begged an invitation to dinner at the house of a little friend with whom he had been play- ing during the morning. At the table, his hostess inquired anxiously, "Randolph, can you cut your own meat?" "Humph !" said Randolph, who was sawing away, "can't I? I've cut up quite as tough meat as this at home!" "We don't want no franchise—eve wants a vote!" was shouted out the other day at a political meeting by one of England's future masters. Perhaps the speaker lea descen- dant of the Radical farmer at Dover who fifty years ago refused to vote for Sir John Rae Reed. "No," he said sturdily, "I'll never support no man what votes against animal Parliaments and universal suffering!" GEOGRAPHY TO SOME PURPOM—Dinner Table.—Little Millie (to her father, who has given her the smallest piece of pie on the plate)—" Papa, why is my piece of pie like Europe ?" Papa, thoughtfully :"I don't know; why is it ?" Millie : "Because it is the smallest of the grand divisions," Fact. PRESSIOG HOME.—They were walking in the conserva- tory at the last White House reception. "Will you love me with all your soul ?" she murmured. " Yes, darling," he answered. "And all your heart?" " Yee, dearest." "And all your—" "Everything, darling, everything," he interrupted. "Pocketbook?" she continued, not noticing the interruption. He gasped once and all was over. WHY HE PAID IN ADTANCE.—A traveller in Shasta coun'y, Cal., being belated, stopped at .a country hotel and put up for the night. After eating his supper, he asked the landlord how much it was. "What yer have ?" "Liver, ham and eggs, potatoes, bread, and coffee." "Three dollars." "Here you are. Ahem! Have you any bolts to your bedroom doors?" "Yes, bolts and keys, too." "I guess I'd better pay you for my lodging and breakfast now. I always eat a hearty breakfast, and if you charge for it like you did my supper, I vien't have anything left for any one to steel if they get into my room." As a large ocean-going steamer was making her way to her moorings in the Mersey, the officer in charge found the passage blocked by a dirty empty ballast barge, the only occupant of which was Bitting down smoking a short pipe. I Finding he did not make any eft:art to get out of the way, the officer called out in tree nautical style to the man. Taking the pipe from his mouth, the fellow rose and said, "An' is it yerself that's the captain o' that ship?" " No," was the reply, "but lam the chief officer." "Then talk to your wells," said Pat; "I am captain o' this!" A PALPABLE MISTAICE.—Mrs. Smith: "I am very sorry, Mrs. Hendricks, but I consider it my duty to inform you that I saw year hueloand coming out of a saloon last even- ing." Mrs. Hendricks: 'What time was it, Mrs. Smith ?" Mrs. Smith: "About eight o'clock." Mrs. Hendricks: "Did yo a say he was coming out or going in ?" Mrs. Smith: "Coming out." Mrs. Hendricks (positively) : "You have mistaken him for someone else. John never comes out of a saloon as early as eight o'clock." HIS GAISE WOULDN'T WORE—Judge Peterby came home not long ago pale as a ghost and trernbeing all over. "What's the matter ?" asked his wife. "Mad dog bit me. In less than two hours I'll be raving mad and snapping at everybody who comes near me." "Judge Peterby," said his wife, calmly, "you can't work that little game on me. Ma is going to stay right here in the house and help me te take care of you." "I expect I'll have to go and be treated by Pasteur," said Peterby. "Ma and I will go along with you." Up to the time of our going to press Peterby has de- veloped no signs of hydrophobia, but to say he is mad is no exaggeration whatever. SHE PAID EXTIM—A widow, whose age might have been 40, went into business on Grand River avenue a few weeks ago and the first move was to get a sign painted. The services of a sign painter were secured, and when he finished his work he put on his "Imprint" by placing his "W. A. H.," down on the left hand corner of the sign. When the widow came to criticise the work she queried: "What does 'W. A. H.' etend for ?" "Why, • Wanted, A Husband," replied the painter." "Oh, yes—l see," she mused. "It was very thoughtful in you, and here is a dollar extra!" • The late King Ernest of Hanover was very abstemious, and usually had the best of health; but, if on occasion his doctors prescribed medicine, Put it in the cupboard!" was the order when the physic came. Once his majesty was really ill for several weeks. As any bottle or powder was brought, relates the Rev. C. A. Wilkinson, the king's cheplaitt, his majesty said, "Put it in the cupboard!" and again and again it was "Put it in the cupboard!" Not one drop was touched. Starving and patience were the only remedies resorted to. At last his majesty got his good turn, and began to feel he could eat again with a relish; and by degrees nature flung off the disorder, whatever it was, which had run its course. His majesty was up and dressed early, and at business. "Get all those bottles, powders, and pill- boxes out of the cupboards," he said, "and range them in a row round the room." It was a very small room, and they almost made a circle round the walls. The doctors came in, smirking and smiling, and congratulated the king upon being up again and looking so well. "Yes, doctors," said his majesty, "thank God it is so! But look there—count it I up! Don't you think, if I had drunk all that infernal stuff, t I should have been dead long ago?"

FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE AT NEWTON. A large and interested congregation assembled in St. Peter's Church, Newton on Monday forenoon, when the marriage was celebrated of Miss Isabella Best McCorquodale, the seventh surviving dausrhter of Colonel George McCorquodale, JP., of the Wil- lows, Newton. to Mr. Josph Hume Dudgeon, 8.A., stockbroker, second son of Mr. Henry James Dudgeon, of The Priory, Blackrock, Dublin. The church had been appropriately adorned, and the passage from the gates to the entrance of the church was carpeted for the occasion. Special seats were reserved for the wedding party and guests, and the well-earned popularity of Colonel McCorquodale and his family was clearly evidenced by the large attendance of well- wishers and friends. In addtion to Colonel and Mrs. McCorquodale, there were also present: Mr. A. C. Mc- Corquodale, J.P.. Mr. and Mrs. Geo. F. McCor- quodale, Mr. and Mrs. Dudgeon, Dublin (the bride- groom's father and mother), Colonel Hamilton, M.P., Mr. W. F. Gooch, J.P., Mx. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., Mr.l T. H. Pearson, Dr. J. W. Watkins, Mr. R. L. and Mn Greenshields (Liverpool), Mr. H. F. and Mrs Birley (The Mount, St. Asaph), Mr. and Mrs W. C. Jones, Mr. and Mrs Blacklock (Newnham Hall, Daventry), the Rev. R. Smith, rector of Lowton, Captain and Mn Withington, and other ladies and gentlemen. The interesting ceremony was performed by the Rev. ner- bort Monk, M.A. (vicar), who was assisted by the Rev. Henry Sherlock, formerly vicar of Haydock, (brother-in-law of the bride) and the Rev. George T. Stokes, professor of Ecclesiastical History in the Uni- versity of Dublin, and brother-in-law of the bride- groom. The bride, who was given away by her father, Colonel McCorquodale. wore a dress of white satin trimmed with Brussels lace, with a wreath of orange blossoms, with diamond ornaments. She also carried a magnificent bouquet. The bridesmaids, who were attired in white muslin dresses, with bows and veils, and each carrying a bouquet formed of daffo- dils, were Miss Edith McCorquodale, Miss Hamilton, Miss Dudgeon, Miss Nairne, Miss Cox, Miss Bald, Miss Greenshields Miss Mary McCorquodale, and Miss Sher- lock. Mr, 'Wilfred Fitzgerald officiated as best man. The service in church was of a choral character, and pleasantly enhanced the proceedings. As the party took up their places in the chancel the con- gregation united in singing the hymn, "The voice that breathes o'er Eden," and at the conclusion of the ceremony the organist fine- ly rendered Mendelsaohn's "Wedding march." On leaving the church the happy aouple were received with the most cordial manifestations of good wishes, and flowers were strewn along their path. The guests, who numbered 126, afterwards Ea down to a " break- fast," of the most sumptuous character at the Wil- lows. the magnificent bridescake for which had been supplied by Messrs. Bolland, of Chester. In the afternoon the newly-married pair left for London, en route for the continent. The presents, which were of a most costly characterand very numerous, included the following :—A diamond pendant to the bride from the bridegroom, three stars from Mr. G. F. and Mrs. McCorquodale, a pianoforte from Col. McCorquodale, Brussels lace from Mrs. McCorquodale, hall clock from Colonel and Mrs. Hamilton, table silver from ' Mr. and Mrs. Blacklock, silver tea and coffee service from Mr. A. C. McCorquodale, china desert service and diamond ring from Mr. Norman McCorquodale, desert knives and forks from Mr. Harold McCorquodale, afternoon tea set from Mr. and Mrs. R. L. Green- shields, claret jug from Mr. and Mrs. H. F. Birley, bacon dish from the Rev. H. and Mrs. Sherlock, ruby and sapphire bangles and ring from Mr. and Mrs. Dudgeon, and over 120 others. To each of the brides- maids the bridegroom presented a safety pin and brooch with pearls and sapphires. Mr. Thos. Birtles, Warrington, was commissioned to take photographs of the bride and bridesmaids and of the whole party ; and we understand that he was successful in obtain- ing a considerable number of good plates.

_ ITHE NEWTON LIBERAL "300." A meeting, called by circular, of the Council of the Liberal "800" of the Newton Division of South West Lancashire will held in the Co-operative hail, Earle-street, Earlestown, on Monday evening. The business was the consideration of Mr. Gladstone's measures in regard to Ireland, and to pass a resolu- tion thereon. There was a good attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. C. Pilkington J.P. (vice-president), who was supported by Messrs. G. •W. Rawlins (Rainhill), F. A. R. Neill (Bold), P. Hall (Eeriest own), R. M. Campbell (Registration Agent), &c. At the commencement of the proceed- ings the Chairman drew attention to the presence of representatives of the Press, and expressed the opinion that the proceedings should not be re- ported, with the exception of any resolution which might be adopted. Tie formally took the sense of the 'meeting thereupon, and his view was supported by those present. The Chairman after- wards delivered an address dealing with the ques- tion, and said he hoped the matters would be calmly and carefully discussed, as they were met on a very important occasion.—Mr. F. A. R. Neill (Bold) then moved "That this meeting recognises that the time has come for a permanent settlement of the Irish problem, and believes that in the prin- ciples of self-government, embodied in the Govern- ment of Irelani Bill, the Prime Minister offers such a solution of the difficulty; and therefore thanks Mr. Gladstone for his measures, both of Government and .Land Purchase, expresses its un- abated confidence in the Government over which he presides, and assures them of its earnest support in the present crisis." (Applause.)—The motion was seconded by Mr. G. W. Rawlins (Rainhill), sup- ported by Messrs. C. A. Luffman, L. T. Foulkes, M. Birkhead, J. Prescott, &c., and carried unani- mously. The substance of the resolution was directed to be telegraphed to the Prime Minister in 1 the House of Commons, and it was also decided to : call a public meeting on the subject."

NEWTON VOLUNTEERS AT LIVERPOOL.—The visit of her Majesty the Queen to Liverpool during the present we, k has afforded the Newton Volunteers an opportunity of taking an active part in guarding their Sovereign. On Tuesday forenoon 12 members of the F Company of the 19th L.R.V. (Liverpool Press Guards), under Colour-Ser- geant Henry Houghton and Sergeant Bateman, left. New- ton Bridge Station by the 20 minutes past 11 train, and during the afternoon farmed part of the guard of honour to the Queen in the International Exhibition. On the follow- ing forenoon at the same time 82 men of the F Company journeyed to Liverpool. In the absence of Captain Wood (through illness) they were commansied by Sergeant Instruc- tor Parks and Colour-Sergeant Houghton, and there were also present Sergeants Bateman, Percival, Aitken, and Roberts. When they arrived at Liver- pool they were marched to the head-quarters of the battalion in Everton-road, where they joined the rest of the men. The battalion started from the head-quarters about half-past two, and lined Lord-street and Whitechapel. Her l'il.,jesty passed through their ranks on returning from her sail on the river. The men were dismissed at Lime-street station, and returned at their own convenience.—Tbe New ton company of the 9th L.R.V. also took part in the demon- strations. They met at the drill-yard, Vitriol-square, Earlestown, at noon on Wednesday, under the command of Captain Tnomsen. There were five sergeants (Haselden, Tunstall, Dolan, Seddon. and Fitzgerald, with Sergeant- Instructor McCoy) and 38 men. They left Earlestown by the one o'clock train for Warrington, where, at the drill ball, they joined the rest of the battalion. They afterwards proceeded by special train to Liverpool, and they lined London-road when the Queen returned from her sail. The local volunteers partook of refreshments at Liverpool and Warrington. div.head: :LOWS to the gditor.
div.p: :LOWS to the gditor.
TliE CLOVEN HOOF.

Irieh-N-a--tion-a—list numbers, we are told, are not only eetirely reconciled to bani,hment from the Imperial parliament. but strongly object te have the honour of TAM- berehip thrust upon them. Could anything be more preg- nant with meanteg to those who wish to clearly understand all that may be involved in the Irish question than this face? The English people, I take it, are thoruughlv tired of the Irish question, and to settle it they would not be nig- gardly in their conces•ions to the demands of the dissatis- lied Irish. coeld they feel assured on the one point that those eonct•sAiona would not be turned into weapons to injure this country. Self-preservation is the first law of nations as of individuals. In this case self-preservation imperati,elv demands that Ireland, no matter how self- governing she may be, must nut be a separate independent state. An independent state means a possibly hostile state with power to make that hostility felt, and with an inde- pendent and hostile Ireland the geographical and political conditions which have so materially helped to make Eng- land what she is would disappear. England's naval and Military forces would be so needed to preserve the heart and centre of the empire that the chances are that it would fare but ill with the extremitiee in time of need. The mode of dealing with the Irish problem then, it seems to me, really depends upon the answer to the question : Is it the ulti- mate aim of the Irish Nationalists to remain for weal or for woe part of the empire or to establish an independent country? It is because the strong objection of the Irish Members to have Any representation at Westminster points to an answer to this question that I regard it as being so inn of meaning. For why should they object to have a voice in the affairs of the empire if they sincerely desire to remain part of that eamire ? If they stick to this objection it must become clear as daylight to everybody that their secret aim is separation. The cloven hoof of their real in- tention will than be easily seen behind the thin veil of their very recent protestations.

rriß "SHOP HOURS" BILL. Sit,—However disinterested the witnesses from the large West-end concerns in favour of Sir John Lubbock's Bill, they are open to the charge of advocating their own in- terests. their object being to compel their weaker competi- tors to do that which they themselves have already &tie voluntarily. For myself, I yield to no man in my desire for a more squat distribution of the drudgeries and delights of life, but I have no sympathy with any line of action which shows a disposition to bring undue pressure to bear on the crueby taxed small shopkeeper, by whom, with his limited returns. and heavily weighted as he already is, the cramping effect of uncalled-for State interference would be keenly felt. We know it is commonly contended by persons who know nothing of trade, that as much business can be done in eight hours as in 12, and therefore that if all close at a given hour ne one will be the loser, but it seems to be forgotten that this necessitates a larger staff, and hence incressen working expenses, resulting in a corresponding loss, unless covered by larger gross profits, by no means uniformly attainable. Local legislation, however, in the form of by-laws for the regulation of specific trades would be far preferable to pet- , titogging Imperial legislation for young persons under 13 years of age, which wculd seriously interfere with the or- der of busieess, would prejudicially affect the relations be- tween employer and employed, and certainly tend to ex- clude such young persons from employment, the law itself becoming a dead letter, unless made effective the ugh the agency of an army of inquisitorial inspectors. Let the hard-working shopkeeper contemplate with equanimity, if he can, having to submit to the visits of these well paid, easy thing. bureaucratic gentlemen ! Moreover, it is patent to all that the health of youth is quite as critical from 18 ;o 21 as from 15 to 18, not to speak of the fact that applicants for employment, whether adults on their own account, or guardians on behalf of minors. make his hours of business a main factor in their negotiations with an em- ployer. The data upon which it is proposed to legislate are a compilation ef greatly exaggerated statements, intermingled with palip.hie falsehoods, and constitute a glarine libel upon the British ehopkeeper, many of the alleged cases of injury te health Isom business being to the candid mind obviously the result of inherent delicacy of constitution. Only on Saturday last an article in the "Spectator" afferded a striking illustration of the misgui,led zeal which prompts so many to attempt to grapple with this question. who from ignorance of the facts are quite unfitted to do so. The writer says, amone other things, that the work of serving in a shop is more monotonous than work in a factory, and is therefoie more injurious to health! Surely the most super- ficial observer of the two cccupations must be aware that this is an absurdity. I challenge the writer of this article to name a vocation, in wit:eh a corresponding number of women, of similar calibre, could find employment as varied and remunerative, and so little prejudicial to health, as that afforded by the dry-goods trade. Hasty legislation on this question is above all things to be deprecated. It is not for a few prominent London traders to act as if they were competent to represent the trading community throughout the kingdom, and to endeavour to slip through the House of Cernmona this ill-digested measure. It behoves shopkeepers all over the country to bestir them- selves, and to insist that the circumstances of ali be duly considered, whether it be the fashionable business in Bond- street or the chandler's shop in Bethnal Green.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, JOHN LEWIS. Oxford-street. W., May 7, 1886.

div.head: SOCIAL REVOLT.
div.p: THE SOCIAL REVOLT.

Sir,—" The chie—fest authors of revolutl ns have been Not the chimerical and intemperate friends of progress, but the blind obstructors of progress : those who, in tietiaoce of nature, struggle to avert the inevitable future, to recall the irrevocable past." The above words were written by Mr. Goldwin Smith near upon twenty years ago. Read in the light of the events of to-day, they seem to carry a sig- nificance to which too much importance cannot possibly be attached.

It has been said" that a contented people never rebel." Wheee, then, shall we look fur a contented people ? For rebellion, active or passive, meets our pee at every turn. It seems almost, to the casual observer, that the records of history during the past forty years will be made up of efforts on the part of the struggling masses to assert their eight, and to lay claim to their inheritance to a share in the benefits arising from nineteenth century civilisation. Those who oppose this just aspiration of the people are they who are struggling to avert the inevitable future, and are strain- ing every nerve to recall the irrevocable past—are in fact the sole cause ot the Social Revolt as seen in Ireland, Russia Germany, America. and England. Mr. G. J. Holyoake, in his " Hietory of Co operation," and referring to Carlyle, says :—" Future revolutions would be bloodier than heretofore through his teachings." He preached the doctrine of despotism, and could forgive mur- der, if the criminal was a strong man like Governor Eyre. The right of the strong to rule is being challenged. Trafal- gar-square and the West End ef London were recently made to witness this; manufacturing Belgium and the Ger- mean autocrat have bad within the past few weeks a rude awakening, and have been compelled to recognise the fact that it is not a natural state of things for one man to spend hie life in unremitting toil, to have considerable difficulty in securing the means of subsistence for himself and family, while another man, ganging everything by the easy circum- stances to which be was born, is solely governed by his own leersonel standard of happiness, and rests content to find himself able to dip his Lands into an inexhaustible pocket, who can command luxurious residences at home and abroad, and tualiraited sources of personal excitement and amuse- ment. Thinking men have been startled by the recent events in Chicago, and following so soon upon similar disturbances in other lands, will, perhaps, ask themselves the question, what 13 the cause of thie uneasiness on the part of the peo- ple? and bow shall we End means to allay It? It may b 3 that in future, in times of tracte disturbance, we shall no more be told of the danger of interference with capital, or that unless labour shows a more amenable disposition capi- tal would take itself off to a more reasonable part of the world. If labour is poor and rooted to the sfen, capital is not in much better plight. Invested in valuable plant, to translate it to other lands, means serious loss. The duration of the present period ot "Trade Depres- sion" has existed for at least ten years; indeed, since the year 1831 the year of the great London Exhibition. We may reckon that the strides made by other countries, in what were, before that time, considered British trades in man- ufacturing for home use and exportation have seriously crippled the home trade. British trade is crippled bentese it is surrounded and hedged in by old and selfish land laws; and persisteecein these laws will tend to spread through the land revolutionary ideas ; Socialist agitators will be listened to with avidity, men will not be content to walk about the streets three and four days a week, year in and year out. The times are out of joint; employer and work- men have broken away from each other ; between them stands one whose sympathies are bought and paid for by the capitalist, whose greatest aim in life is to know that a satisfactory dividend has been declared, and that his awn prosperity is assured. You may wander through street after street in our manufacturing towns and not find the residence of a single manufacturer-;-" all, all are gone." Municipal matters are left to the care of half-educated men, or to men whose interest at stake is not sufficiently large to prompt them to adequate exertion. The science of politics is of so dismal a character that its votaries are recruited from the climes only who are depending and hoping for Parliamen- tary reform as a means of alleviating abnses. The one touch of nature that ehould make the whole world kin seems to becoming small by degrees and beautifully less, and requires some extraordinary convulsion to make itself apparent to the tmpoetic mind. Next week, with your permission, I will carry this matter a little further.—yours,
H. WHITHAM.

THE ALLEGED OUTRAGES AT F.ARLESTOWN. —On Saturday a large number of persons assembled at the Town Hall, Newton, in the expectation of hearing the trial of two youths charged with cri:ninally assaulting little girls under circumstances reported last week. The magistrates decided to take the evidence in private, however, and for this pur- pose, at the conclusion of the other business, they retired to their ante-room. Robert Jones, 16 years of age, living in Gas-street, and an apprentice at the glass bottle works, was charged with criminally assaulting his sister Elizabeth, nine years of age, at their home, in January last. He was Committed for trial at Liverpool Assizes.—Charlea Eaves, 15 years of age, was also committed for trial at the Assizes. on a charge of criminally assaulting Elizabeth Sturges,, NMI years of age, at the Vulcan, on Sunday week.

THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAT 15 1886 SHOCKING FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE RAILWAY. On Thursday morning, shortly after midnight, a postman named James Buckley Mellor, met with a tragic death on the railway near Bank Quay Sta- tion. Part of the duties of deceased was to take a number of mail bags about midnight to a little wooden cabin which is erected on the railway in the direction of Arpley Bridges, and there assist in sort- ing them and afterwards in suspending them on an apparatus in order that they may be taken up by passing mail trains. The cabin stands within a few feet of and faces the down line, and in front of it there is a sort of low wooden platform, which reaches within two or three feet of the rail, and On which, it appears, deceased was in the habit of ar- ranging his bags, while a companion was similarly engaged in the cabin. When thus employed, de- ceased used to kneel at the side of the platform nearest the rails, so that his body would probably as a rule be within the reach of the footboard of a train on the down line, if he did not remove from his position in time. Just after midnight, on Thursday, he was engaged in his usual work with a companion named Goodfellow, and it is supposed that he was unexpectedly caught in the dark and rather stormy nigh by a tourist train which went past the cabin at the time, be- cause he was missed by his companion directly after the train had gone, and his mutilated body was shortly afterwards found lying on the line some dis- tance away from the cabin, and in the direction the train was moving in. The remains were taken to the Wilson Patten Hotel, at which place an inquest reported below was held. Deceased had been in the employ of the postal authorities in Warrington since 1873, and had been for many years a member of the 9th Lancashire Volunteers. With his corps he had taken part on Wednesday in the celebrations at Liverpool in connection with the Queen's visit to that town, so that his death occurred soon after he. returned home. He wad married, and lived at 5, Arpley:walk, Friar's-green, Warrington. The inquest was held at the Patten Arms Hotel, yesterday afternoon, before the coroner, Mr. Brig- house. The inquiry was watched on behalf of the police by Inspector Berry; on behalf of the Post- master-General by Mr. Buckton ; and on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company by Mr. Ferrand. Previous to calling witnesses the coroner and jury paid a visit to the scene of the fatality, and inspected the box and apparatus which are used in connection with the mail service. Hav- ing returned to the Wilson Patten Hotel and viewed the body, the first witness called was Jonathan Buckley Mellor, father of the deceased, who gave evidence corroborating some of the above-mentioned particulars. He last saw his son alive, he said, on Wednesday night, about 20 minutes to 11 o'clock, in Sankey-street, deceased being then going to his work.—James Goodfellow said he was employed at the Warrington Post Office as a postman. He and deceased were at Bank Quay station together on Wednesday night, and deceased left about a quar- ter to 12 o'clock, with nine bags for the•mail box. He (witness) left the station for the box about ten minutes past twelve o'clock with three•bags, and he found deceased at the cabin when he got there about a quarter-past twelve. In the ordinary course of events, their duties at the cabin ended at thirteen minutes to one o'clock, and during the time they were there they had to make five pouches up, each pouch taking from four to five minutes. When the pouches were made up they were hang on the catch of the apparatus to be taken away by the train. When -*itness got to the cabin deceased was working at the outside, which was his recog- nised place, as he (witness) worked inside. The last time he saw decoas-d he was engaged putting his bag on the pouch, being in a kneeling position. About that time the down tourist train passed the cabin, and his attention was attracted by the vibration of one of the bags, but he did not see deceased. As it was a rule when a train passed for the man to go round to the back of the cabin, or -come inside, he expected to see deceased come back again, but when lie did not come he shouted for him, there being, however, no answer. Witness then went outside with his lamp to look for de- ceased, but not finding him he went across the line to see if the pouches for the "up. special" train had worked all right, and fol And it had. He afterwards went up the ladder at the apparatus, and there caught sight of a piece of deceased's shirt down the line. He went in that direction, and found de- ceased's body about forty yards from the cabin in the 4-foot of the down line with his head facing the station. Ile could not tell which shoulder had been struck, if either of them had been. He (witness) had been engaged eight or nine weeks at that special work of taking mail bags to the cabin and making them up, and deceased had been engaged at the same work all that time. Thirteen was the general and largest number of bags they had to make up, and eleven was the smallest, and the longest time they had in which to make up the pouches was about 25 minutes. Two persons could not work in the cabin at one time. He should say the distance from the outside of the cabin to the outer rail of the down line was about 7 feet, and from the edge of the wooden platform the dis- tance to the rail would be, he thought, about 18in. —By Inspector Berry: Deceased never complained to him about the danger at that particular spot, but he (witness) made the bags up inside the cabin, know- ing there was a danger outside. Witness had never complained of the danger to any of the Post Office officials. He had never seen any rules or regula- tions saying they must not work outside the cabin. If the cabin were larger and the door instead of facing the lines were reversed there would. be no danger—By Mr. Buckton : There were instructions posted up in the cabin as to how they were to work the mail apparatus, and he knew deceased had seen those instructions. There was a footpath behind the apparatus on the very edge of the embankment for their safety in passing to and from the cabin. He could not say that it might not be 2ft. 9in. from the edge of the platform in front of the cabin to the nearest rail. The train that took their bags was due at 1244 a.m.—By the jury: The bags they had to carry to the cabin would weigh sometimes between 40 and 501b5., he thought.—The Coroner then pointed out that the instructions referred to by Mr. Buckton did not say the men were to work in the cabin.—A Juryman remarked that it would be impossible for two men to work in the cabin.— In answer to further examination, witness said

deceased was perfectly sober on the night in question, and fit for duty. They could not hear a train coming that night. It was also stated that deceased had been engaged at the post office since 1873 and had been engaged in this special work about two years.—Wm. Hard- staff, the driver of the train which was supposed to havo killed deceased, said he did not know anyone had been killed by his train until, he reached Car- lisle. At the time they passed they passed the mail cabin they would be travelling at the rate of about forty miles an hour. At Carlisle he examined the engine and did not find a sign of blood or flesh. They had no instructions to whistle before they reached these mail cabins.—Wm. Taylor Hunt said he had been employed at the Post Office about six years. For !".) years he had performed the particu- lar duties referred to, Goodfellow succeeding him. He considered it rather dangerous walking from the station to the cabin, and it was dangerous working outside the cabin. Deceased used to work outside the cabin as he preferred to do so because he could make his bags up more quickly. He (witness) had never complained officially about the danger of working outside the cabin. He could not answer why he left that particular duty, but it was not be- cause he found it unsafe, nor did, he ask to be re- moved.—By a Juryman : He had seen pieces of iron flying about when a train passed. —The Coroner : I suppose you considered that a mere matter of detail ?—Witness said there used to be a much better road from the station to the cabin, but now they must either walk on the main line or go over a large number of rods. He had had bags to carry that weighed about 701bs.—Mr. Buck- ton having mentioned that the cabin was really for shelter for the men, and that there were places used for similar purposes where there were no cabins, the Coroner, in addressing the jury, said that al- though he did not wish to intrude his opinion to his mind it seemed that although every precau- tion. had been taken for the safety of the men at the apparatus where the pouches were put, it seemed as though the hut was constructed ao as to court danger rather than avid it. Its dooropened right on to the hue, although it was quite open for the door to be put on the other side or at the sides. It seemed to him that all danger at the spot would be obviated by turning the cabin right round.—The jury having then been left for a few minutes to consider their decision, a verdict of.accidentaldeath was returned, with a recommendation that a cabin large enough for the accommodation of two men be constructed for the use of the mail messengers ; that the door be put at the side: that .a proper way from Bank Quay Station to the cabin be provided, the present way being dangerous; .and that all trains approach- ing the cabin give a. signal for the benefit of any person using the cabin.

foreign manufactured silk and woollen goods, imperted iron, steel, leather, alkali, paper, glass, embroideries, watebee, lace and other articles should be taxed twenty per cent. This would give the Chancellor of the Exchequer £9,330,000, the halt of which be suggested should be ap- plied to the reduction of duties mentioned in his resolution. —Sir W. CUNLIFFB Bnooxes seconded the resolution. Mr. Cobden, he said, prophesied that all nations would become free traders in five years. Nearly ten times that period had passed, and it was time for us, if there appeared to be no probability of other nations following our example, to turn round and take our own course.---Mr. G. BovreeL contended that any proposal to revert to the old and dis- carded policy of Protection was misleading and mischiev- ous in its tendency. It was opposed to the best interests of the trade and commerce of the country, and injurious to the welfare ef the working classes. Those who wished to prevent foreign competition should propose to place a duty on the export of machinery and of coal. lie thought if manufacturers had studied more the quality of the goods they produced, the present state of things would not have existed, which, in his opinion, arose from the markets being flooded with cheap and inferior prodections.—Mr. BAUMANN thought a great mistake was made when pro- tective duties were abolished.—Mr. S. SMITH believed Fee Trade was a matter of life and death to this country, as we had to import food for one-half of our population, and pay for it with manufactured goods. It was necessary for us, therefore, to cultivate cheap production in order to ob- tain command of the neutral markets.—Mr. A. Colereoa. referring to the evidence taken before the Commission on the trade depression, showed that landlords were getting rxceseive rents, while indastry was suffering.—Mr. L. BAKER contended that on the whole the condition of the labouring classes had improved Anne Free Trade had been established.—Mr. J. MacLEare could not vote for the amendment. There was a widespread feeling amongst working claims that foreign competion bad a very great deal to do with the present depression; but be did not think that was a feeling to be encouraged by imposing duties en the imports of foreign manufactures.

BIRTHS AND DEATHS IN WARRINGTON, &c. The Registrar General states that during the quarter that ended on 31st December last the mar- riages in England and Wales happened at an annual rate of 16.5 per 1,000 inhabitants, the mean of the ten years, 1876-85, being 17.9. The present rate is the lowest one for the fourth quarter of the year since registration began, in 1837: Further, the mar- riage rate for the entire year 1885 is 14 4, and this appears to be the lowest one since 1879, when the same ratio existed. These are the two lowest rates on record since 1837.

In the quarter that ended on 31st March last the births in England and Wales occurred at an annual rate of 33.6, which is 1-5 below the average of the first quarter in the ten previous years. The death rate is found to be 22.8, and this appears to be 0.6 above the mean of the ten years. This is the. high- est March rate since 1879. This rise is probably due to the great fatality of diseases of the organs of respiration; at any rate, the death rate by in- fectious diseases fell to 1-9, against a mean of 2.3 in the ten previous corresponding quarters. Small- pox, scarlet fever, and fever of other types were all much under the average, while whooping cough, measles, diphtheria, and diarrhoea were over it. Cold weather checks the progress of zymotic disease but, of course, increases the mortality by diseases of the organs of respiration. Now according to the meteorological return from the Royal Observatory,. Greenwich, the mean temperature of the air in the past quarter was 30.5, or 2-3 degrees below the average of the corresponding quarter in 115 years. The excess of births over deaths in England and Wales is 73,737, against 92,549 in 1884 and 84,104 in 1885. Of the emigrants leaving 21,539 were Eng- lish, 3,460 Scotch, and 6,093 Irish, English and Scotch emigration having slightly increased, while that of the Irish was lower than in the first quarter of any year since 1879. In the three months that ended on the 31st March last there were 731 births and 419 deaths registered in the district or union of Warrington, the latter total occurring against an average of 371, taken from the three previous corresponding periods. There were 114 deaths of infants under 1, and 102 took place at 60 and upwards. There were 35 deaths re- corded in public institutions, 17 were inquired into before the coroner, and 12 were due to violence. The fatal cases of the principal infectious cases were :—Measles 2, diphtheria 2, whooping cough 25, fever 1, diarrhcea 7. This is a very assuring return for the past quarter, for although the deaths from all causes are seen to be in excess of the average, the zymotic diseases, with the exception of whooping cough do not appear to have contributed to this result. The long continuation of low temperature has 'existed very markedly in most districts, but in the case of Warrington this is not so plain. In the Newton sub-district the deaths were 83, or 1 more than the average. Measles, diphtheria, and fever each caused 1, diarrhcea 3, and whooping cough 7. In Winwick district there were 7 deaths, or 1 more than the average, while in San- key district 13 are returned, or 3 less than the average. In neither of these dis- tricts was there one death by an infectious disease. In Warrington sub-district there were 477 births and 275 deaths, 50 more than the average. Whoop- ing cough caused 17, diphtheria 1, and diarrhcea 4. In Latchford district there were 25 deaths, 2 less than the average. Whooping cough caused 1. In Rixton district there were 13 deaths, 1 over the aver- age. One was due to measles. In Lancashire the births in the past quarter reached 3.3,255, this agreeing very closely with the average of the three previous corresponding quarters, which is said to be 32,904. The deaths numbered 23,303, showing an excess of 1,925 over-a similar estimate. As many as 2,612 deaths took place in workhouses, hospitals, and other public institutions. and 612 were due to violence. The fatal zymotic diseases were—Small-Pox 31, measles 736, scarlet fever 261, diphtheria 1-09, whooping cough 599, fever 262, and diarrhcea 324. Of the small-pox cases 25 were returned for the district of ,Toxteth Park, 1 for West Derby, 1 for Manchester, 3 for Ashton, and 1 for Blackburn. Measles were chiefly fatal in Wigan, Blackburn, and Barrow districts. Diph- theria caused 26 deaths in West Derby and 16 in Chalton. Fever cases figure in most of the district returns, but the total is not at all high. In the dis- trict of Toxteth Park, West Derby, Wigan,,Warring- ton, Bolton, Bury. Rochdale, Haslingden, Black- burn, Treston, and in a few other places, the deaths were in excess of the average for the quarter, but this is without allowing for increased population.

div.head: FNIENDLY SOCIETY CASE.
div.p: FNIENDLY SOCIETY CASE.

At the BOrough Court, yesterday, Reuben B. Ditch- field and William Henry Taylor, local collectors of the Liverpool Victoria Legal Friendly Society, were summoned for withholding certain books in their possession from the Society.—Mr. W. 11. J. Jenkins appeared for the society, and Mr. Wallhead (from the office of the Town Clerk) was for the defence.— In opening the case, Mr. Jenkins said the proceedings were taken under the Friendly Societies Act, 1885, section 18 of which provided that if any agent, &c., withheld any pro- perty of a society he was committing an offence under the section. The two defendants had for some years past been enraged as collectors for the society, which had branches in various towns in Eogland, one eT which was in Winwick- street, Warrington. A round, as it was called, that formerly belonged to Mr. Edwin Roberts, the defendants took up sunder certain conditions. Mr. Roberts had been an old and faithful servant, and the society thought it incumbent on them to make some provision for him in his sicknees. The round was banded over to the defendants, on the under- standing that there Phould be a rebate or allowance which went as a provision for Mr. Roberts Defendants, it should be stated, had attended well to their business, and ford given every satisfaction, therefore the society had no fault to find with them; but havieg no fewer than 4,000 persons in their employ the society were obliged to rule them somewhat with an iron hand, and the rules were ex- ceedingly strict. The books were the property of the society, and notice bad been given to the defenilants to hand them over, but they had refused to do so. The arrangement dur- ing the illness of Mr. Roberts was that tbe defendants should be allowed 25 per cent. of their collections as re- muneration. subject to what he (Mr. Jenkins) might term rebate in favour of the late Mr. Roberts, to form a fund for his maintenance. Taylor was to allow 16s per week and Ditchfield 8s 6d per week to go into the fund. When Mr. Roberts died, the society felt they would be paying the de- fendants more than they ought if they allowed them to re- ceive the whole payment, and the Committee of Man- agement granted them 15 Der cent, on their receipts. Mr. Tattersall. a travelling agent of the society, was deputed by the Committee of Management to take the matter in hand and, in an interview, conveyed to defen- dants the determination of the society. Defendants, how- ever, declined to accede to the 15 per cent arrangement. They wrote to the Comrnittee of Management to the effecc ' that there had been an Worms' demand made upon them for their books, which they resisted, and that on making ' their calls they found that two persons had been collecting money from the members. They asked that an end should be put to such annoyancee, which were hurtful to the society and disagreeable to the agents. The defendants' • letters were taken into consideration, the Committee of - Management wrote to Mr. Tattersall, and the culminating point was reached when the defendants received notice of dismissal, and they declined to give up the books of the enciety.—Mr. Jenkins was about to call evidence, when r Mr. Wellhead raised technical objections as to the absence I ot proof of the appointment of Mr. Tattersall'as agent, and I also asked for the production of the minute books of the

' THE FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT. Last evening the deputation appointed at a meet- ing held, a few weeks ago, at the Horsemarke t- I street Coffee Tavern, waited by appointment upon the Library and Museum Committee to urge the , desirabilty of opening the Lending Department to the public free of charge. The deputation included Messrs. Thomas Morris, 11. Whitham, .1. Winstanley, J. Wild, J. Walker, and J. Gandy, and was intro- duced by his Worship the Mayor to Mr. Beamont (who occupied the chair) and to the Committee. It was urged by various members of the deputation that it was extremely desirable, in the interest of the whole community,,that the Warrington Library . should be put on the same footing as most Public Libraries in the kingdom—namely, that books , should be lent out free of charge. It was admitted that the reading-loom was very valuable, but what was wanted in addition was that readers and stu- dents should be able to read at home. The growth of education amongst the young caused reading in the family circle to be of special importance. It was pointed out by the Chairman and others of the committee that the books , of the Library were lent out to any inhabitant who . thought fit to pay is 6d per quarter or 5s per year; and that, as the subscriptions from this source brought in about £l5O per year, the committee did not see their way to dispensing with this sum and making the Lending Library 'free by depending on the £530 received from the rates. It was a question mainly of ways and means, for, to begin with, the committee were some £2OO or .E3OO in debt as a re- sult of the extensive alterations and improvements which had recently been made. With regard to this side of the question, one member of the deputation said he thought the difficulty could be overcome if they were willing to put their shoulders to the wheel; and he wished to know whether, if money were forthcoming to pay off the present debt, and a scheme clevised to meet the loss from abolishing the subscriptions, the Committee would undertake to set the Lending Library free. The Chairman said the committee could not pledge themselves under any contingency of that kind; for the Library could not be made absolutely free without incurring additional expenditure. Touching the subscription of 5e per year, the deputation sub- mitted that, though not large on the face of it, it was quite sufficient to act as a bar to the poorer class of ratepayers. Where there were two or three readers in a family of different ages and dif- ferent tastes, it meant 10s or 15s a year. There was nothing of the kind in other towns in connec- tion with the Public Libraries; and it was thought that the time had come when Warrington Library should be placed in as good a position as the rest. Some conversation took place on a sug- gestion which had been made by a member of the ' committee for making the Lending Library free, on the understanding that subscribers after buying their own books with their own money might hand them over to the Library at the end of a year; but the committee did not think this would meet the difficulties of the situation. The deputation left without coming to any understanding with the committee. It may be added that the deputation ' will report to a general meeting to be held at the , Horsemarket-street Coffee Tavern, at eight o'clock on Tuesday evening, to which all persons are in- vited to attend who are favourable to the movement for freeing the Library.

EXTRAORDINARY DEATH OF A GIRL.—A girl named Elizabeth Lumoley, residing at 47, Mustard-street, Glod- wick, Oldham, has met her death under singular circum- stances. She was eating some bread and jim, when a small flint stone stuck in her throat. A doctor was called in, gild performed a surgical operation in order to extract the stone, but the girl died two hours after swallowing the cone.

A son of the man by a former marriage was called, and stated that in 1808 his father murdered his first wife by stabbing her, and that he was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to ten years' penal servitude. The jury found that Thomas Donohue murder his wife, and suscquently committed [do de se DIE STORM: GREAT DAMAGE.—In consequence of the recent heavy rains serious floods have occurred all over the country, causing enormous damage to property. Several districts were on Thursday and Friday visited by a terrific gale which caused further destruction. Railway and tele- graphic communication over a very wide area has been seri- ously deranged or entirely interrupted. In the hill districts snow has fallen, sheep have perished from exposure by the score, and in the low lying country almost equal havoc has been wrought amongst stack, oxen, seep, and pigs having been caught in the swollen torrents and drowned. Amongst the rivers which have overflowed their bmks are the Trent, Derwent, Monnow, Wye, Rea, Rother, Tame, Dee, Stour, and Severn. In some districts rain has fallen continuously for three days and nights.
LORD HARTINGrON AND HIS SUPPORTERS. MARTING AT DEVONSIIIRI3 HOUSE.

A conference of those members of the Liberal and Radi- cal parties, who find themselves unable to follow Mr. Glad- stone in his proposed legislation for Ireland, was held at Devonshire souse, the residence of the Marquis of Har- tington on Friday afternoon. The circular calling the meeting was issued by Lord Hartington to both those who follow him and those who act with Mr. Chamberlain, and it is understood that altogether 130 invitations were issued. Members commenced arriving at D,vonshire House shortly before noon, and up to that hour about twenty had entered, including Mr. Albert Grey, Mr. Elliott, Sir Julian Goldsmid, Sir John Lubbock, Mr. Heneage, Mr. P. Rylands, Mr. Saunders, Lord E. Cavendish. Mr. Caine, and Mr. Trevelyao. A small crowd of spectators have gathered outs:e the house. The crowd outsiie the building had considerably augmented during the preceding half hour, but the people appeared more humorous than en- thusiastic. Mr. Cnamberlain drove up in his carriage shortly before one o'clock, and WAS almost the last of the members to arrive. The meeting Was a large one, though some of the Radical dissentients to whom invitations were sent did not attend. Tne proceedings at the meeting were private but the Central News learns that Lord Hartington, In addressing those assembled, declared that the atenclance at that meeting ',lmplied a distinct disapproval of the pro- positions of the Government respecting Ireland. The num- ber of Liberal members who had declared their intention of voting against the second reading now made the rejection of the measure a certainty. He e.id not regard that as a triumph, for it cast upon them a very heavy responsibility, which, however, th.,:e were quite prepared to accept.—Brief speeches followed, in all of which it was utged that the first duty of all present was to oppose the bill. It was agreed that the opponeets of the bill were not called upon to for- mulate any alternative scheme' but the expression of Opinion was that any plans for Ireland should be such as would be applicable to other parts of the country. Towar is the close of the meeting Lord Hartington admitted that the introduction of these measures of Mr Gladstone had mate- rially altered the situation, and would make it necessary to review the whole position before any definite proposals could he made.—Mr Charn4erlain, Mr .Treyelyan. and Mr Itylands briefly addressed the meeting, and they referred to the Land Bill as a part of Mr Gladstone's scheme, which it might not be possible to detach if the Home Rule meacure were carried. The number of members attending the meet- ing was 64. Mr. Chamberlain remained behind after the meeting had broken up, and bad some conversation with Lord Hartington. • _ _

Later in the evening' the Central News learns that com- munications passed between Lord Hartington and Mr-Glad- stone, and his lordship also had a very long conference wkh Mr. W. H. Smith at the House of Commens. During the evening ths Premier was in communication with prominent members of his party, and with certain of the party mana- gers.

' 1111. GLADSTONE AND THE riarr.r. In reply to a representation by Mr. Illingwortb,M,P, on behalf of Liberal members favourable to the Government's Irish scheme, proposing a meeting of the party to discuss the present position of affairs, Mr. Gladstone has for the presone declined the proposal, on the ground that it would probably accentuate existing differences, unless HOMO de- finite suggestion were to be put before the meeting. THE DIVISION.

Unless the supporters of the Government on the Liberal benches deliberately prolong the debate, it is probable that a division will be reached by next Friday, or by Tuesday week at the latest. The Irish members do not intend to intervene largely in the discussion, and there is a strong desire on the part of the opponents of the bill that the division should be taken as early as possible. 4"
DARING OUTRAGE IN PARTS.

PARIS, FRIDAY.—Last evening a man entered the office of the Bataan Loubeyran, director of the Banque D'Escomte, and, preeenting a revolver at him, forced taint to sign three cheques for £2 000 eacta. He then decamped. The culprit is an absconding agent named Piliot, who has been guilty of forgery. 11113 GREAT STORK IN THE UNITED STATES. A Central News telegram, dated New Yank, Friday morn- ing, states:—The details of the great storm are still incom- plete in consequence of the wholesale destruction of iele- graph wires, but sufficient information has been received to show that the storm extended over all the central States. Ohio experienced the fall fury of the tornado, and has suf- fered more than any other State, about twenty towns baying been devastated. Brooks were in a few minutes swollen into torrents, and rushing onwards with irresistible force carried away houses, trees, animals, and everything that lay in their course. Several railway trains came to grief through the washing away of the embankments. Details reachinc here every few minutes only add to th e long list of those killed.

LAST -NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at 4 o'clock. Lord LONGFORD presented a petition from the inhabi- tants of Nottingham praying that a system of State aided emigration be set on foot.—A number of petitions against the Irish Government Bill were presented.—The National Debt Bill was read a second time. • Their Lordships adjourned at 4-30. PC.2 HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. QUESTIONS, &c.—Mr. Hiestitax gave notice that on an early dny be should move a resolution for the payment of Income fax collectors by salary instead of poundage.—Mr. H. FOWLER, replying to Mr. Vanderley, said the case of the Civil Sorvice writers was now under consideration. He could net say when a decision would be arrived at.—Mr. Brows. replying to Mr. Baden Powell, said under the new Spanish Convention goods manufactured in the British colonies entering Spain, or Spanish colonies, would enjoy the most favoured nation clause. THE FAIR TRADE QUESTION. On the mixion to go into into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates Mr. JENNINGS, as an amend- ment, moved that in the opinion of the House it was expe- dient to raise a large portion of the revenue of the country from import duties, and that such duties should be levied on certain descriptions of fully manufactured foreign goods entering into competition with similar goods of our own make, and that the revenue so obtained should be applied to to the reduc.ion of the duties on tea, coffee, and cocoa and other burdensome imports. He strongly Insisted that, in the present state of depression, it was imperatively necessary we should take some steps to rerneiy the present unfortunate state of things He con- tended that the whole condition of our trade has been altered since 1856. Mr. Cobden told them foreigners, could send us corn and take oar manufactures in exchange. but that anticipation had not been verified. It had been stated tbatweweredeterminednotto alter our present system and foreigners applauded our determination, and it was evi- dent their reason for that leas that it made their industries flourish, no matter what became of ours. WARRINGTON AND THE QUEEN'S VISIT. On Tuesday morning the Queen, accompanied by several members of the Royal Family, passed through Bank Quay Station on her way to Liver- pool to open the International. Exhibition there. The royal train left London soon after midnight and reached Warrington punctually to the minute at 7-20 in the morning. Her Majesty was cheered by the persona who were on the platform as the train passed through. The train containing the Queen and the Royal suite passed through Warrington on the return journey at 10-30 on Thursday morning. Great care was taken to keep the platform at Bank Quay free from people. A considerable number as- sembled on Froghall-lane and Bank Quay bridges, and at other places near the railway, With the hope of obtaining a glimpse of the royal personages. On both Tuesday and Wednesday large numbers of persons left the town for Liverpool by the two railway lines. On the latter day over 1,700 people booked by the Cheshire lines, in addition to the Warrington and Newton members of the 9th Lan- cashire Rifle Volunteers, who went to take part in the reception of her Majesty. Preparatory to their active duty, the corps paraded on Monday evening to be exercised in the movements to be performed on the Wednesday following. There was a very good muster. On Wednesday they assembled at headquarters at one o'clock and went by special train to Liverpool at 2-15. Colonel Greenall being appointed Brigadier, the command of the corps devolved upon Major Bolton, who very efficiently fulfilled the duty. The following officers were also present :—Major and Adjutant O'Leary, Captain Bridge, Captain Ridgway, Captain Widdows,Captain Thompson, Captain Gooch, Captain Buckton, Lieu- tenant Baynes,Surgeon Gornall, and Quartermaster- Sergeant Hutchinson. There were also 33 sergeants. 22 corporals, 12 buglers, 3 permanent staff, and nearly 400 privates. On arrival at the city the corps fell in, and marched to the College Grounds, where they were provided with refreshments. The men did duty all the time under a heavy down- pour of rain, and were literally wet through and through. They arrived back at Warrington at about eight o'clock, being conveyed in a special train. They proceeded to the Drill Hall, where they were complimented by the Colonel. Refresh- ments were served, and, after giving three ringing cheers for the Queen, the men dispersed. It may be mentioned that the Warrington corps at Liver- pool met with much commendation for their sol- dierly bearing. The playing of the band of the corps was also much admired.
